articles.title: DSA Scores Election Victories Across California: From San Diego to Humboldt, membership gains fuel increased activism and wins
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: The returns are (mostly) in, and DSA-endorsed candidates for elected offices from local school boards to the U.S. Congress have been elevated throughout California. A ton of hard work went into this critical election cycle, boosted on the one hand by DSA’s swelling membership, which is now numerically the largest of any socialist organization in the country’s history, and on the other hand by the understanding that in order to stop the march of fascism we had to win big. A half dozen cities in the Golden State are now led by DSA mayors, including the largest one. DSA has become a recognized political force, drawing praise from our coalition allies and dismay from our opponents. Below are reports from ten California DSA chapters on their local election efforts. Humboldt Humboldt DSA endorsed cadre candidate G Mario Fernandez for his re-election bid for Eureka City Council. We were keen to emphasize the contrast between Mario—a DSA member and self-described anarchist—and his opponent, a Republican police officer noted for participating in violent suppression of the local pro-Palestinian student movement. We mobilized our chapter members as well as Mario's supporters among local trade unionists for a grassroots-focused ground game. Between door knocking and phone banking, we banked an estimated 1000 voter interactions. We are proud to report that Mario is currently more than 100 votes ahead at the time of writing, November 17, although results are not yet certified. Sonoma County In February 2026, Sonoma County DSA endorsed our first-ever electoral candidate, Joanna Paun, for County Board of Supervisors. This process reactivated leaders in our chapter who had figured in other electoral victories, such as the Green Party majority in Sebastopol, Omar Fateh’s Minnesota State Senate race, and door-knocking for Prop 50. It also activated a passionate, largely new membership base who believed in the power of ordinary people to challenge the capitalist class. Our opposition was well-funded by real estate, Big Ag, the Sheriff, and corporate consultant Rob Muelrath, who is behind four of the five sitting County Supervisors and numerous City Council seats. We knew it would be near-impossible to get representation for workers when the candidates for office were already beholden to corporate interests. With not a moment to waste, we mobilized our members. We organized weekly weekend door knocks that saw Joanna win 42% of the primary vote—and defeat her main opponent in their home precinct. We organized phone and text banks, made in-house video and graphic content, posted regularly on social media informing locals about the election, and continued activating members to join the campaign. We also released our first-ever Voter Guide in just our second year, in which our Electoral Committee analyzed our county’s races beyond just Joanna’s. This voter guide, combined with our presence in our communities, helped show Sonoma County residents that politics don’t start with expensive campaigns, but with them. Many of our members had never knocked doors or helped run an electoral race that actually aligned with their principles, let alone whose victory could shape the terrain they live in. For example, Joanna ran with the explicit angle of ending county cooperation with ICE, a major chapter priority we adopted in January. She garnered the support of SEIU 1021 and the North Bay Labor Council, along with over a dozen unions and progressive organizations. During our time on this campaign, our chapter forged a tighter bond with rank-and-file union members and impressed upon local leaders that we are a serious, united force in the county. After the primaries, we took a small break to celebrate our wins and mount our strength. During our primary campaign, we activated over seventy of our members and trained several who would become Field Leads. We proved that the DSA difference is indeed real—that when we unite, we can defeat opponents taking six figures from police and oligarchs with people power, union support, and buy-in among those who feel alienated from the system. We proved that a socialist agenda delivers on funds for schoolchildren, public infrastructure, affordable housing, union empowerment, and human rights for all , not just some. By late summer, we once again hit streets and doors for the general election. By then, we had become involved with our close ally, Teamsters 665, in supporting winery workers organizing a new union in an industry that hasn’t had one in over 40 years. We also organized our local No Kings IV, and our members joined numerous community initiatives to block Flock and other automated license plate readers (ALPRs). The groundwork we laid through our labor support and community connections enabled us to keep pushing in-house content that laid bare the corruption of our opponents while simultaneously showing our candidate’s vision. Our opposition scrambled. They couldn’t find an angle of attack that could stick. Ultimately, no amount of spam texts or shady mailers could overcome our members doing what they do best: talking to neighbors, friends, and family; getting active in our communities; and laying out the real stakes of the race. Money talks, but our voices were louder. As the general election drew nearer, we endorsed two more chapter members in their respective races: Sarah Seitchik Sebastian, a community organizer running for Petaluma School Board, and Caitlin Quinn, a union president running for County Board of Education Area 2. Our chapter conducted joint knocks for these candidates’ campaigns, assisted with communications, shared their literature, and proudly promoted them to our community. When all was said and done, we won. Our unity with unions and community networks overcame half a century of corporate domination in District 2. Joanna maintained a 22-point lead from the first ballot drop, and her opponent conceded within the week. Caitlin’s opponent has also conceded, Sarah is maintaining her lead, and we believe our slate will fully sweep soon. Altogether, we delivered a win not only for the socialist movement, but for the workers and families of Sonoma County—those who call this place home, who raise their children here, who have to move due to the cost of living, who wonder why their services are being cut while developers take public property, who wonder why their government is unresponsive. They won’t have to keep wondering. Now, they will have a progressive majority on the highest body in Sonoma County, allies in office to fight for their interests, and a future that belongs to them. Joanna Paun for County Board of Supervisors: Won by 22% (called) Caitlin Quinn for County Office of Education: Leads by 1% (opponent conceded) Sarah Seitchik Sebastian for Petaluma School Board: Leads by 4% (not yet called) East Bay This sprawling chapter, the second largest in the state and encompassing two counties, played an important role in several municipal elections and state ballot measures, charting ten wins and four losses. On the state ballot measure front, we formed a tax the rich working group at our annual convention in the spring as one of the chapter’s three priority campaigns. The working group met biweekly forward to November. Along the way we collected signatures for what became Props 3 and 40 (won Prop 3, lost Prop 40) and led education and training efforts for the membership, and then with coalition partners Alameda Labor Council and Alliance of Californians for Community Empowerment (ACCE) similar events for the broader community. Later in the summer and fall we canvassed and phone banked with the labor council on the tax the rich campaign, together with our other jointly endorsed campaigns for Oakland School Board (we won one out of two seats we competed for) and Berkeley Rent Stabilization Board (five out of five, giving us an 8-1 majority). We lost Berkeley Measure Z, which would have provided seed funding for a public bank. On City Council races we went two for three, electing 23-year-old student Syrak Micael in Berkeley, reelecting George Syrop to the Hayward City Council, and running a spirited campaign for Oakland District 2 with Nate Adams that fell short. Perhaps our marquee campaign was for mayor of Richmond, where East Bay DSA has had a longstanding partnership with the Richmond Progressive Alliance. We supported two-term councilmember Claudia Jimenez in her run at the top municipal job. In winning 55-45% she became the first immigrant Latina female elected mayor of Richmond, and second DSA member, running on a strong working class-first platform of no corporate contributions, against ICE incursions and standing up to the conservative institutional elephant in the room, the Chevron refinery. Dozens of EBDSA members showed up for her canvassing and phone banking every week. Silicon Valley We are proud to report back on the incredible effort and growth our chapter demonstrated during this recent election cycle. While not every ballot measure went our way, the true victory for Silicon Valley DSA this year was our capacity to organize, mobilize, and build lasting power in our communities. Silicon Valley DSA endorsed Props 3 and 40, and No on 41 and 42. We also endorsed Redwood City Measure E (Rent Control), which lost, 46.25% Yes to 53.75% No. During the last midterm elections, our chapter simply did not have the capacity to campaign for propositions or measures in any significant way. This year, our leaders and volunteers stepped up to effectively organize our own canvasses, generate a social media campaign, and work in coalition with local organizations to reach voters directly. Our impact: Voter Contact: We made 783 voter contacts and knocked on 482 doors. Mobilization: We engaged roughly 51 unique volunteers across our campaigns, with many taking on multiple shifts. Coalition Building: We strengthened our relationships with local partners, including the Peninsula DSA, where we mobilized members to attend external canvassing opportunities. The volunteer data for those canvasses with coalition partners has not been made fully available to us at this time. We are incredibly proud of the foundation we have built this year. Our members learned new skills, our chapter developed new leaders, and we are well-positioned to continue fighting for the working class in Silicon Valley. Peninsula Peninsula DSA organized around five campaigns here in San Mateo County as well as a state level campaign. We endorsed three candidates for local city council: Ofelia Bello in East Palo Alto, Phoebe Venkat in Foster City, and Melanie Olson in South San Francisco. We also endorsed Measure E to establish stronger rent control and tenant protections in Redwood City, advocated for the Regional Transit Measure to fund and maintain public transportation, and endorsed the statewide Billionaire Tax through Prop 40. Members supported these races by gathering signatures to get the measures on the ballot, then ahead of the general election fundraising, going door knocking, dropping literature, phone banking, text banking and creating and distributing our own voter guide. Earlier, in 2025 Peninsula DSA successfully convinced the SamTrans Board to opt into SB 63, ensuring that the Regional Transit Measure would be on the ballot in 2026. We were saddened to see both Measure E and Prop 40 fail, as well as Phoebe and Melanie defeated by their corporate-backed opponents. However, we celebrated Ofelia finishing first in a crowded field and look forward to a socialist on the East Palo Alto City Council. The Regional Transit Measure also passed, keeping buses, trains and subways running throughout the Bay Area. Central Coast This general election cycle, Central Coast DSA went 3 for 3 on our endorsements: defeating Measure Q, a 7% utility users tax in Marina; defeating Measure H, which would have repealed several renter protection ordinances in Salinas; and electing our candidate for Marina City Council District 4. Our chapter ran its first cadre candidate for office, chapter co-chair Athena Rita Burciaga, and won. The membership showed up: by the end of the campaign, fifteen members were turning out to canvass, out of a chapter that now has 150 dues-paying members. Athena’s win was a comeback. On election night she was in third place with 29% of the vote, 81 votes behind. As the late ballots were counted, she climbed into first and now leads with nearly 36% of the vote, a 54-vote margin, pending certification on November 25. Many voters saw Mike Simmons, a moderate Republican, as a Democrat, and the results showed he was splitting Athena’s voters far more than those of the other Republican in the race, Brad Imamura. We overcame that by knocking on every door in Preston Park and Abrams Park, Marina’s renter neighborhoods, and the late ballots from those neighborhoods broke decisively our way. We won by running an unabashedly socialist campaign: protecting renters, building a future young people can afford, and taking on the corporate interests that have held a firm grip on Marina’s local politics for too long. On December 15, Athena Burciaga will become the first transgender person to take elected office in Monterey County. Santa Barbara DSA Santa Barbara worked very hard this election cycle in our local city races. As a smaller chapter, we decided our efforts were best used in local elections. Santa Barbara has a city council comprising six members elected through districts plus the mayor, the only citywide representative. Three city council seats were up for election as well as the mayor’s position. In June and July, a couple members of our electoral working group decided to start meeting with the most progressive candidates to discuss their interest in receiving our endorsement. This culminated in a chapter meeting where we had all the interested candidates inform us about their positions and answer questions. At that meeting we ended up endorsing two city council candidates but postponed our decision for the other two. At a special chapter meeting, we endorsed both remaining candidates, meaning we had endorsed a candidate for every district election as well as for the mayor’s seat. Following our endorsement process, we mobilized and canvassed hard. For the first few weeks we canvassed every Saturday morning. This was in partnership with the local Democratic Party, which in Santa Barbara is run by a democratic socialist; they had endorsed all the same candidates. We decided to participate in their canvassing efforts because of their access to voter information, including the PDI mobile app. Around six weeks before the election we halted our biweekly electoral working group meetings in favor of weekly door-knocking campaigns. The Santa Barbara Tenants Union did the same; they are very close allies to our chapter. We abandoned the strict rules of canvassing that the Democratic Party followed and focused on apartment complexes that had worked with the Tenants Union in the past. These seemed to be our most successful efforts, especially because of the recent passage of a rent stabilization ordinance. It’s hard to say how many doors we reached as an organization, but it is in the thousands if not tens of thousands. We averaged about three to five people every Saturday and around ten for every Wednesday canvas, including the Tenants Union members. We led canvassing events, talked to constituents about elections, posted on social media, and made a voter guide. But mainly we organized and went door to door. All of this effort resulted in all of our endorsed candidates winning their races: Devon Wardlow for City Council District 4, Ian Baucke for City Council District 5, Gabe Escobedo for City Council District 6, and Kristen Sneddon for Mayor of Santa Barbara. Sneddon was outspent by hundreds of thousands of dollars. This cycle created a six to one super majority on the Santa Barbara city council in favor of progressive politics (four of whom openly call themselves democratic socialists). For many of our members, this was their first time canvassing. We mobilized many new members, increasing our chapter’s knowledge and abilities for future campaigns. At the same time, we built new coalitions with allied organizations which we look forward to developing further post-election. Inland Empire The primary effort of Inland Empire DSA in the 2026 elections was to rally support for our endorsees Joz Sida and Joe Alvanez, and to a lesser extent the campaigns for Propositions 3 and 40, and No on 41 and 42. This work was carried out by the Electoral Committee, recently formed in November 2025. In prior years the chapter had no designated space for electoral organizing. As a result, inexperience was the primary hurdle IE DSA had to overcome throughout the election season. There was a lot of learning involved, but we are happy to report victories for Joz Sida (Mayor of Fontana) and Joe Alvanez (Fontana City Clerk). IE DSA facilitated our endorsements by the creation of a Voter Guide , phone banking, canvassing, tabling, and our Tax the Rich Rally on October 10. The voter guide was created by the Electoral Committee's Voter Guide subcommittee in just under two weeks and was released to the public October 12. It was a tight timeline, as we wanted to have the voter guide out ASAP, as ballots were being filled and returned as early as October 1. Nonetheless, the voter guide was one of our big successes, as it filled a void left by other left leaning political organizations in the Inland Empire. We have heard many reports of non-members using and sharing it, and it has been mentioned by new members during onboarding. Phone banking efforts focused on IE DSA membership. The goal here was to activate paper members by getting them to come out for electoral work. On this front, there was much more success with events centering Joz and Joe compared with the YES on 3 and 40/NO on 41 and 42 campaigns. The prospect of a local IE DSA elected seems pivotal here. In-person canvassing efforts received relatively low turnout but were instrumental in developing member organizing skills and IE DSA as an electoral organization. The canvassing process did this by familiarizing members with PDI & Solidarity Tech apps, and face-to-face conversations with the public contributed to the chapter's presence in the Inland Empire. Tabling efforts took place at voter info events in Cal Poly Pomona and a No Kings rally in downtown Riverside. IE DSA’s presence at these events was well regarded and conversations with the public were consistently positive. Throughout the election season, people were incredibly receptive to DSA politics. We made it a point to hand out lit for “Workers Deserve Better” alongside the propositions at these events. Another success came from the Tax the Rich Rally, held on October 10th in downtown Riverside (part of the statewide “Tax the Rich Day” events with DSA and organized labor). Riverside is the center of the IE’s democratic politics. Its central location, diversity, public transportation, and overall population made it the obvious choice for the rally. We were helped by SEIU-United Health Workers organizer Gabe Montoya, who also served as a guest speaker. Our other guest speaker was recently elected assemblywoman Clarissa Cervantes, a self-proclaimed DSA-aligned progressive and major force in Inland Empire politics. IE DSA is ecstatic to report victories in the form of our endorsed candidates Joz Sida and Joe Alvanez (we are in the process of establishing a Socialists in Office committee), relationships built between the chapter and the Inland Empire’s progressive organizing scene (namely Clarissa Cervantes, the Working Families Party, and Party for Socialist Liberation), and most importantly, the growth of the chapter Electoral Committee and development of its members as organizers. Going forward, IE DSA’s electoral goals lie in the cities of Riverside, Moreno Valley, Fontana, and Ontario, and the bulk of electoral work in the following months will happen in our newly formed research subcommittee. We are in a much stronger position than we were at the start of the year and expect that strength to continue on into 2028. We believe the Inland Empire is ripe for democratic socialism, and plan to run cadre candidates for city council and mayoral elections in the central cities. Orange County Santa Ana is a Red Zone!!! Following successes that socialists have gained just in the last year, OCDSA has also grown to unprecedented heights with record membership numbers! To Californians, Orange County is infamous for rank conservatism and development company corruption, but at the heart of the county there are immigrant and working class communities that face brutality from the police state (alongside those other two problems). The OC chapter didn’t have an electoral committee at the beginning of this year, but the bump in membership due to the ripple effects of Zohran Mamdani’s victory gave rise to a newfound capacity within our chapter to knock 10,000 doors within three months and sweep all four endorsed campaigns: Ben Vazquez (Ward 2), Sandra de Anda (Ward 4), and Isuri Ramos (Ward 6) for Santa Ana City Council, and Measure D for ranked choice voting in Irvine! Ballooning housing costs alongside the fascistic presence of Trump’s deportation troopers translates to the hollowing of what makes Santa Ana exceptional. Santa Ana has been a cultural hub for our immigrant communities with a vibrant art scene and inclusive night life, but it's in the midst of a housing crisis that has pushed out working families. All three candidate campaigns touched on the fight against data centers and police accountability in the midst of a very violent year for the SAPD to name a few of their common policy priorities. Before the election, chapter organizing in the city was primarily centered around our Immigration Justice and Mutual Aid efforts. Since its creation, OC DSA's Immigration Justice Committee has engaged in direct action, organizing Know-Your-Rights canvasses and strengthening OC's ICE watch and mutual aid network, notably at day labor corners found at Home Depot and U-Haul parking lots. For a worker-centered alternative vision for the Orange County we deserve, local organizing based in socialist principles serves as the North star for our most powerful electoral campaigns. Council Member-elect Sandra De Anda serves as the Director of Policy for the Orange County Rapid Response Network (OCRRN), a grassroots organization rooted in a mutual aid model to center the dignity of affected community members and combat the debilitating effects of ICE actions throughout the county. De Anda has credited much of her campaign's success to DSA’s unprecedented approach to mass organizing—what she has proudly called the “DSA difference”! While De Anda has fought tirelessly for sanctuary policies from the outside of city council for years, with her local DSA chapter's backing, De Anda will soon be co-governing from inside the halls of power. Santa Ana’s housing crisis requires a new look at city planning policies that help lower the cost of living, and councilmember-elect Isuri Ramos’s work on the Planning Commission as a supporter of rent control and a data center moratorium made our endorsement a logical decision. Her advocacy for immigrant and tenant rights will ensure a strong voice on council for communities targeted during these anxious economic and social times that Operation Metro Surge has instilled in the city. Her time as the executive director at Chispa, a local organization fostering Latinx youth political power, speaks to her depth of knowledge in the material conditions of the immigrant and working-class communities. We also picked up an institutional powerhouse with Councilmember Ben Vazquez. He became a DSA member during his second run for council, and his time as a teacher and teacher’s union vice-president make him a valuable ally for the left and for Santa Ana. As a teacher, he ensured that students received a history education that helps students reflect on society down to the material realities of their day to day. His expertise in city council politics and time in labor organizing provides the language and mechanics of governance for our socialist majority’s toolbelt along with a political compass in line with our values and mission. These skills will provide incoming councilmembers with the tactics to match their passion alongside the remaining city council. On top of these great wins in Santa Ana, Irvine's Measure D for ranked choice voting won in part by activating our local YDSA chapters to get them acclimated to campaign organizing. This ensures that incoming membership has the people power and working-class organizing skills needed to upend the previously entrenched establishment in city governments across the county. These victories are a stand against the police unions that collude with I.C.E. and the surveillance state that inflates city budgets for the oligarch class. Although important, these council victories are not the end of the organizing work. The Trump administration’s recent appointment of Stephen Miller to Chief of Staff doubles down on domestic policy like Operation Metro Surge. With a new, progressive mayor in Dan Shimell replacing conservative mayor Valerie Amezcua, change has come, and DSA members are in a position to carve a new vision for Santa Ana at the heart of Orange County. San Diego In 2026, DSA San Diego’s electoral work was focused on two spring campaigns and three campaigns during the General Election. Our electoral efforts were focused on base-building in central San Diego while hammering out wins in farther flung cities within the county where working people are being stretched thin at the gas pump and by politics centered around corporate greed. The movement has found its foothold in North County San Diego, with two endorsed candidates winning their races in the region: Joey Aszterbaum for Trustee of MiraCosta Community College Area 6 and Kenneth Zuniga for Mayor of Vista! DSA San Diego's membership initially focused on two ballot measures—one local and one statewide. We initially canvassed in support of Measure A, a local measure that aimed to tax vacant homes in an effort to encourage more housing to be put on the market and to collect revenue to help combat homelessness. While it failed at the ballot, we mobilized 100 people to reach 2,831 doors. We then collected signatures to get the Billionaire Tax on our November ballot; we reached over 1,200 doors and collected 115 signatures at the door. During the General Election, we ramped up our efforts and focused on bringing home wins for one consolidated statewide ballot proposition campaign and two candidate campaigns. Our proposition campaign to Tax the Rich (TTR) advocated for constituents to vote YES on Propositions 3 and 40 and also vote NO on Propositions 41 and 42. Prop 3’s passage continued a tax first put in place in 2012 on high-income earners to fund education, while Prop 40 advocated for a tax on individuals with a net worth of more than $1 billion to fund healthcare as well as education and food-assistance programs; the latter failed to pass. Propositions 41 and 42 were put on the ballot to nullify the Billionaire Tax if it passed; Prop 42 passed. DSA San Diego’s TTR campaign was primarily based in the City of San Diego with some broader outreach to the southwestern region both inside and bordering the City. TTR saw the chapter’s largest walks on average with each canvass seeing just over 20 volunteers and the largest seeing 32 volunteers. Over the course of seven canvasses for TTR, 144 people knocked 3,486 doors. Prop 3 passed and Prop 40 failed. Our candidate campaigns were focused on two cities in the County of San Diego: El Cajon and Vista. Alexander Kraft ran as a third-party socialist candidate to unseat incumbent Republican Bill Wells in the City of El Cajon. DSA San Diego mobilized 115 people to knock 2,996 doors across 11 canvases. Kraft outperformed Wells’ previous Democratic challenger by more than 14 percent, receiving 43.64% of the vote in a city where Wells had previously won with 70% of the vote., Although Kraft lost his race, the incumbent won by tighter margins than previously seen. While registered Republicans edge out registered Democrats among El Cajon’s electorate, DSA San Diego’s endorsed race in the City of Vista was playing out in a city with more registered Democrats despite having a Republican mayor. DSA member Kenneth Zuniga ran against former Vista Councilmember Joe Green. Across the 12 canvasses co-hosted by DSA San Diego, 110 canvassers were mobilized to knock 5,481 doors. Zuniga won his mayorship, becoming the first democratic socialist mayor in the County of San Diego!

articles.title: L.A. Socialists Turn Electoral Wave into Governing Power
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: LA Mayor-elect Nithya Raman “LA was at a critical cusp in its history. Globalization had reorganized its economy, rewiring it in dramatic ways, and many people were being left behind. Yet the city had—and still has—this incredible, protean potential for better things, for progressive politics, for surprising activism.” – Mike Davis The midterm elections were truly seismic. Like many places across the country, Los Angeles made good on its protean potential from the 2026 blowout with a stronger socialist movement and a larger share of political power. DSA members won up and down the ballot. Nithya Raman has famously won the mayor’s office of the country’s second largest city in a upset victory. Marissa Roy has won the city attorney’s office, and Angela Gonzales-Torres is headed to Congress. Together, their victories put democratic socialists in two of Los Angeles’s most powerful citywide offices and send a DSA-LA member to Congress for the very first time in a race that few expected a year ago would even be a close challenge. The formerly conservative, sleepy suburb of Burbank has elected a DSA council majority, the first on the West Coast and one of only two places currently in the country. Behind those wins is DSA’s second-largest chapter. In the last year alone, the LA chapter doubled its membership to over six thousand members, launched a citywide Shake Up LA slate, and knocked more than 110,000 doors. And it did so alongside a realignment of the city’s left-labor coalition, especially that of the powerful hotel workers union UNITE HERE Local 11, which cross-endorsed most of DSA-LA’s Shake Up City Hall slate from Nithya down to Burbank city council and whose thousands of members knocked doors for her. In the midterm elections, democratic socialists won two of Los Angeles’s most powerful citywide offices and sent a socialist to Congress from the city for the very first time, in a race that few expected a year ago would even be a close challenge. National Earthquake Of course this didn’t happen in a vacuum. Nationally Democratic candidates of all stripes won control of both chambers of Congress, while Republicans lost ground in a shocking 99 percent of roughly 2,100 counties where most ballots had been counted by Wednesday morning, according to Reuters. The electorate shifted left nearly everywhere, all at once. Early voter surveys showed the multiracial and generational breadth of that rejection. The AP Voter Poll found that about 90 percent of Black voters, roughly 60 percent of Latino voters, and a whopping 70 percent of voters under 30 supported Democratic House candidates. Tufts University’s CIRCLE research center also reported Democratic majorities among young men and white youth, groups that had favored Trump in 2024. Within that national revolt, Los Angeles voters were also shifting left. Gonzales-Torres decisively defeated Democratic incumbent Jimmy Gomez, winning 62 percent of the vote while running openly as a DSA member, supporting a free Palestine and the abolition of ICE, and rejecting corporate money. Her victory gives DSA-LA its first foothold in Congress and demonstrates that a candidate can take clear positions against corporate power, state violence, and yes Palestine and the BDS movement while building a winning electoral coalition. Roy’s victory carries a historic mandate as well. With more than 695,000 votes and 68 percent support she received the largest vote total ever won in a Los Angeles city election at any time, according to her campaign . She campaigned uphill against the Democratic establishment and real estate lobby’s support of the incumbent on turning the City Attorney’s Office into the city’s largest public interest law office: pursuing abusive corporate landlords, enforcing workers’ rights, holding polluters accountable and challenging the Trump administration in court. Alongside Raman’s victory, her election gives DSA-LA its first citywide Los Angeles wins and an opportunity to put substantial public resources behind people confronting powerful interests. Raman’s mayoral victory expands that opening considerably. Her 2020 City Council victory helped establish DSA-LA as a force in city politics. Six years later, she has defeated incumbent (and one-time New Leftist) Karen Bass to become Los Angeles’s first democratic socialist (and immigrant) mayor. Her victory puts a democratic socialist at the head of the country’s second-largest city , giving the movement a new scale of power to advance housing, tenant protections and public services across Los Angeles. (A continuing ongoing tension will be between her independence as an elected and the co-governance and criticism of both the LA Chapter and in DSA’s national leadership about her level of support for the BDS movement). The chapter has also consolidated its existing beachhead in LA city council. City Councilmembers Eunisses Hernandez and Hugo Soto Martínez and LAUSD Board Member Rocío Rivas all won reelection. In the Inglewood area, Estefany Castañeda retained her seat on the Centinela Valley Union High School District board, while Yaritza Gonzalez won election to the Inglewood Unified School District board.(Ysabel Hurado, a DSA member, also retained her seat on city council). Red Burbank The chapter’s reach also expanded beyond Los Angeles. In Burbank, victories for Mike Van Gorder and Nolan Southerland created a democratic socialist council majority alongside Konstantine Anthony, while Stephen Post won in West Hollywood . Estuardo Mazariegos’s race in Los Angeles’s Ninth Council District remained unresolved as of this writing, with Mazariegos trailing by a mere 87 votes after taking on an opponent backed by major corporate and police-union spending. The scale of the work behind these campaigns matters. In its largest electoral effort to date, DSA-LA endorsed 13 candidates and mobilized more than 1,700 volunteers to fill over 4,000 canvassing shifts. Its members knocked more than 110,000 doors in chapter-led canvasses. Over the same period since the 2024 election cycle, membership grew from nearly 3,000 to more than 6,000–and has added several hundred new members since Election Day alone. DSA-LA Cochair, Sean Wakasa, at the 2026 May Day rally The Long Arc The chapter’s program places this strategy in a longer history of multiracial working-class struggle, from Justice for Janitors in the 1990s to the immigrant rights marches of 2006 and the teachers’ strike of 2019. Those movements demonstrated how organized workers could reshape Los Angeles’s politics and advance demands benefiting the wider public. For today’s socialist movement, that history underscores the importance of maintaining an independent organization capable of keeping workers mobilized, turning electoral gains into power, and holding elected representatives accountable– ( a hot button issue with the recent debate and fallout over Nithya Raman. Combining electoral work, movement activism (from anti-ICE mobilizations to mass transit to Palestine solidarity work) and member growth points toward a way to build durable socialist organization—and power. “We engage in electoral campaigns not only to change how Angelenos think about politics, but also to emphasize the role everyday people can play in shaping our world”, said Chang. “Our goal is to democratize decision-making and put power back in the hands of working people. The organizing principles that we implemented across the chapter in this past election cycle form the foundation of mass movement building. An endorsement backed by thousands of volunteer shifts creates opportunities to develop new organizers and leaders, forge relationships with neighbors, and bring people into a member-run organization. She continued: “​I​n turn, the skills our members developed over the last few months can ​be used to strengthen tenant organizing, labor fights, and to defend immigrant communities.​ Each election can leave behind a stronger organization capable of taking on larger fights if we remain committed to organizing our fellow working class neighbors​ into a political program, rather than just mobilizing communities to knock on doors or vote.” Los Angeles is part of a national advance. DSA reported at least eight members elected to the next House: Gonzales-Torres, Chris Rabb, Darializa Avila-Chevalier, Melat Kiros, Claire Valdez and Donavan McKinney, alongside Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib. Its election coverage also recorded state legislative wins in Florida and Tennessee. These wins give the socialist movement more opportunities to connect local organizing with struggles over national policy. There is a wider constituency for that work. Gallup’s September report found that 43 percent of Americans viewed socialism positively, the highest share in its series. In Los Angeles, late-October Berkeley IGS polling put democratic socialist identification at roughly a third of likely city voters. “The democratic socialist constituency is real, and it is growing,” said DSA-LA co-chairs Leslie Chang and Sean Wakasa. The political lesson is that economic demands and solidarity can reinforce each other. Rent, healthcare and wages are central concerns for a working class whose members also face deportation, racism, and attacks on their rights. Workers feel increasingly powerless both inside and outside the workplace. “Workers have been starting to feel that their ability to democratize their voice in everyday decisions such as employment, healthcare, land use, AI & data centers, etc.) are slipping more and more”, said Sean A, a DSA-LA member active in the campaign cycle. “Demands are made and no one listened--until now. This election represents a mandate to return a democratic voice to the working class.” The Promise Gonzales-Torres’s campaign offers a concrete example of how working class politics can be winning politics. Said Sebastian, another DSA-LA member and a super volunteer on the campaign: “This was my first time going out to canvass–much less lead a canvass–for a candidate. Before I met her, everyone would tell me how when you talk to her, it’s not like talking to some politician. We had some great discussions about issues in our community, and she really inspired me to pursue more leadership roles!” The national results alone cannot settle every argument about which message or strategy worked best. They do, however, create an opening for a left that offers more winning, confronts concentrated wealth, and refuses to sacrifice solidarity for supposed electoral advantage. DSA-LA’s experience shows what sustained organization can bring to that opening. The next test will be whether these victories open up more struggles and, most of all, change people’s lives. Roy’s promised enforcement agenda, a stronger socialist presence on city council and Raman’s incoming mayoral administration create openings. Those gains though as always will require organized pressure, alliances with unions and community groups, and members willing to remain involved in the difficult work of governing. They will also take sustained and coordinated pushing and accountability from movements and DSA locally. The promise of the democratic road to socialism is that working people can collectively govern the institutions that shape their lives. In Los Angeles, that promise now has more members, more organizers, and more elected Socialists in Office behind it. The work ahead is to use those gains to keep moving out to the horizon. A version of this story appeared in Jacobin. Reprinted by permission.

articles.title: California DSA’s “Tax the Rich Campaign”: one for two
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: Don’t throw away your pitchforks. You will have more chances to use them in the near future. With the loss of Proposition 40, the Billionaire Tax, by a slim statewide margin of 52.1–47.9%, California DSA’s 2026 “Tax the Rich” campaign went one for two. The other progressive tax on the ballot, Proposition 3, the Education and Health Care Act, won handily, 61-39%. Any attempt to spin the SEIU/United Health Workers-backed Prop 40 defeat as an indicator that California’s electorate doesn’t want to tax the rich—billionaires included—is either uninformed or deliberately misleading. So an obvious question arises: what made the difference in outcomes for the two measures? 400 million dollars from sociopathic billionaires sent a flood of paid advertising sewage across the state A couple dozen of the richest far-right Californians spent close to $400 million to defeat Prop 40—a historic record sum in a ballot measure campaign. Their effort featured scaremongering ads that were outright lies, such as “this is a tax on you” and “Sacramento politicians want to take your retirement savings”. It creatively disguised pure conjecture as expert opinion: “This will end up costing the state more than it takes in”; “All the billionaires will leave”; “Business innovation will be crushed”. Riffing on Pastor Martin Niemoller, we found that first they come for billionaires, and then they come for “you”. These deceitful messages were everywhere throughout September and October—television, radio, digital popups, social media, and in our mailboxes. They buried the purpose of the tax—to prevent three million low-income Californians from losing their health care coverage—beneath a pile of disinformation sufficient to defeat it. The firehose of spending and wall-to-wall advertising moved the needle of public opinion from close to 60% in favor in the spring to just under 50% by November 3. But what exactly did that slight majority of voters vote against? Despite the result, many were not casting a vote against taxing billionaires. Even leading anti-40 voices like Governor Gavin Newsom felt compelled to say that billionaires should be paying more taxes. But in a common dodge for the “No” side of a ballot measure, the messages were “not this one”, because it is “fatally flawed”; and plausible sounding but misleading barbs like “we need such a tax to be permanent and federal, not temporary and assessed at the state level”. And these were the ads that actually mentioned the billionaire tax; most just said “No on 40”, aware that any insertion of the title would remind voters that they hated billionaires. The billionaires’ PAC, “Building a Better California”, threw everything that $400 million would buy at the electorate, betting that with gigantic scale and volume turned up high—and the United Health Workers’ bank account unable to mount an adequate media response—enough of the media sludge would stick to the wall to defeat the measure through stoking fear and confusion. And they were right. On the wrong side Let’s be clear that the billionaires didn’t achieve this result entirely by themselves. Several nominally progressive organizations—the California Teachers Association, Building and Construction Trades Council, and Planned Parenthood—vocally opposed Prop 40, along with Governor Gavin Newsom, steering mainstream news coverage to meekly accept billionaire talking points in endlessly repeating that labor was split, “teachers” (insinuating all teachers) were against the tax, and “progressive groups” were worried that all the billionaires would leave. One thing that didn’t appear anywhere in the mainstream news stories was this angle: CTA, the BTC and Planned Parenthood leadership were opposed to the tax on billionaires. None of these organizations offered a plebiscite to its members, some of whom—like CTA affiliates United Teachers Los Angeles and United Educators of San Francisco—took matters into their own hands and came out in favor of Prop 40 in defiance of their parent organization’s stance. Likewise, the California Federation of Teachers, traditionally the more democratic and progressive of the two statewide education unions, initially neutral through a leadership vote, reversed itself and went pro-40 in September after an internal rebellion at its state council meeting. The California DSA campaign From the moment California DSA passed its resolution in January to support the Education and Health Care Act along with the Billionaire Tax, putting together a statewide tax the rich working group, democratic socialists stood virtually alone in running a united campaign for both measures. The reasons for this have been explained in earlier issues of California Red (see here and here ). Although many of our chapters worked hard to promote both and build a bridge between the two campaigns, it wasn’t until August that we were joined in common cause by powerful players like the California Federation of Labor Unions and the state Democratic Party. In that eight-month stretch we held state and local educational meetings on progressive tax policy in person and on zoom, and trainings on how to effectively hold house meetings and gain organizational endorsements for our dual campaign. We ran articles in every issue of California Red ; created flyers for the joint campaign in four languages and posted them on a one-stop shop “tax the rich” campaign page on our website, ready to download, as well as an FAQ (Frequently Asked Questions) and progressive tax bibliography. Our chapters chartered their own tax the rich working groups. We invited guest speakers to our meetings like Vanessa Williamson, author of The Price of Democracy: The Revolutionary Power of Taxation in American History . We worked with artist Jos Sances to create a beautiful campaign poster and printed thousands at a union print shop and distributed them to the chapters that wanted them. David Solnit led an art build that produced picket signs and banners. San Diego DSA printed “tax the rich” doorhangers for canvassing. After the California Federation of Labor Unions voted at its convention in early August to support both measures, we initiated a collaboration with the state federation to make October 10 “Tax the Rich Day”, with joint rallies and canvassing in eight cities. And over the final weeks before Election Day East Bay DSA staged human billboarding at busy intersections in Oakland and banner drops on freeway overpasses in Berkeley and Santa Cruz. Too late Despite the hard work of DSA members from San Diego to Sacramento, the campaigns for Prop 3 and Prop 40 grew no closer together, and things looked bad for Prop 40 until the beginning of August. At that point SEIU-UHW organizing within two of the major institutions of California progressive politics paid off. First the state Democratic Party leadership, diverging from the governor, voted narrowly to endorse the Billionaire Tax. The next day, with President Lorena Gonzalez leading the charge, the California Federation of Labor Unions at its annual convention came overwhelmingly on board. As icing on the cake, the California Nurses Association joined the newly expanding coalition the following day. But this represented the high point of the campaign. In reality, the labor federation and Democratic Party endorsements came too late to translate into effective support structures and funding. Sporadic earned media emanating from such events as enthusiastic rallies featuring Bernie Sanders and Ro Khanna and cheerleading by Nobel-prizewinning economists turned out to be no match for the record-setting spending avalanche of the other side. A progressive tax campaign needs to hold three cards to have a reasonable shot at winning the game: the right message at the right time; the largest coalition possible, which avoids internal dissension and enables a massive field campaign; and sufficient cash for at least a modicum of paid advertising to augment the ground effort and earned media against the most well-funded opposition imaginable. Prop 40 had but the first one out of three, and it wasn’t enough. With a relatively popular governor actively opposed, and putatively progressive organizations and individuals gravely restating the false messages that billionaires would not have been able to convince the public to believe on their own, the Billionaire Tax had too big a mountain to climb. Compare and contrast with Prop 3’s advantages. Built on a long-standing, extensive coalition of unions and community organizations, with the full backing of the Democratic political establishment (including Newsom, who otherwise never met a progressive tax he liked), and with a bank account supported by the biggest labor political contributor (CTA) in the state, and facing virtually no opposition spending, it offered a free lunch to the public (“not a tax increase”—technically true, just making permanent an already existing tax) along with modestly progressive tax messaging (“if it fails rich people will get a completely unnecessary tax cut”). California DSA can be justly proud of its work to bring together the two campaigns under one roof. But until all parties within organized labor fully absorb and act upon the oldest lesson of labor history—when we are united on issues of common interest for the working class we win, and when we are divided, we lose—campaigns like the Billionaire Tax will find success elusive. Keep the pitchforks handy As for those pitchforks, we can look to two possibilities. Corporate tax increases and/or tax loophole closures could be legislated, and result in enough revenue to reverse the loss of health care for millions of California residents caused by the cruel actions of Trump and the federal government. It’s within the power of incoming Governor Becerra and the legislature to do this. Such tax increases (on income, since thanks to passage of the billionaires’ deceptive Prop 42, wealth taxes are off the table for the time being) would simply require a legislative supermajority of two thirds. If the “blue wave” of November 3 should mean anything to the legislators, it’s that now is the time to act without fear of electoral retribution. The other direction to point your pitchfork is 2028. Already there are rumblings in some quarters about reviving some form of a tax on billionaires. And others are proposing a renewed shot at the split roll tax that narrowly failed in 2020, removing Prop 13 protections for commercial property. Whether early in the new year in Sacramento, or a couple years down the road, your pitchfork will come in handy. Keep its points sharp. [ For a longer version of this article, including a history of progressive tax policy in California, go to Jacobin here .]

articles.title: When We Win
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: Councilmember Van Gorder I take a lot of pride in being a loser. Being a Bernie Sanders supporter will do that to a person: Taking the high road again and again, watching the world get worse, you develop a certain noble toughness. We kept losing, but, hell, we kept our integrity, and we had each other – our one real comfort as entrenched powers kept telling us that our priorities were unreasonable, impossible, or that it just wasn’t the right time. Let the powers that be moderate, we were told. They’d won, after all, so they should know better. Right? And then, of course, when the powerful lost, they blamed the powerless. They couldn’t process their losses. But I always want to embrace my losses, because losing builds character, as the insufferable Dad in Calvin and Hobbes would say. My losing streak officially ended with the rest of the Great Blue Tsunami of ’26 — I was one of three progressives and two democratic socialists elected to the Burbank City Council. We will be joining one conservative and one fellow democratic socialist, making Burbank the first majority DSA city council in American history, and one of the first majority socialist councils since Wisconsin’s Sewer Socialists in the early twentieth century.* The path There are a lot of paths toward the kind of sweeping victory that we’ve just earned, but I can only speak to two: one that I lived, and the other that I watched. My path started in 2017. On Inauguration Day, having processed the shock of a racist game-show host being handed the nuclear football, I decided to make a run at local office with zero resources. If this idiot could do it, then maybe I could, too? Nope. I came in eighth. But I took the connections that I made and founded a tenants’ union in my city. I was alone in attending literally every meeting, and we launched two voter-led initiatives for rent control. Neither succeeded — voter-led initiatives are cartoonishly biased towards moneyed interests, a curse be upon Howard Jarvis and his Smaug-like acolytes. After those failures, a friend asked for help getting a tenants’ union set up in a neighboring city. While I was earning a master’s in housing, that friend, Konstantine Anthony, won a record number of votes in 2020 and became the first democratic socialist elected to his city council. Four years, two kids, a new home in Burbank and a profound financial crisis later, Konstantine asked me to run alongside him as he campaigned for reelection. It was a presidential election year, so the turnout would be high, and that invariably favors progressive candidates, right? Wrong again. He got reelected — I came in fourth. I got calls from folks, institutional types, saying, “You need to run again. Stay public.” They hadn’t backed my ’24 bid, but they saw me knock 3,700 doors and knew my work ethic. I’d built a reputation for consistency. There’s only one way to do that, and it’s being consistent. Staying public wasn’t hard as the federal cruelty machine kicked into high gear. I watched the opposition leaders sit on their hands as hairdressers and restauranteurs were abducted and trafficked to foreign gulags. “What can we do?” the opposition leaders shrugged. “We have no power.” Nature abhors a vacuum, and the absence of a political response from elected officials prompted a popular response. I mentioned the official end of my losing streak being my recent election, but the unofficial end was when the fascist-profiteering airline Avelo made the mistake of relocating its family-friendly hub to Burbank Airport. Using the public profile I’d built during my losing ’24 campaign, I set up one of two weekly protests (neither of us being aware of the other, ironically enough), and in less than three months, the airline bailed not only from Burbank but the entire west coast. Then Jimmy Kimmel hurt Trump’s feelings in September and the Diaper King had Kimmel’s show pulled off the air. I called for a protest on Wednesday night at 9 p.m., and at noon the following day, three hundred people met me outside the gates of Disney to defend free speech. It took less than a week for the government to fold. And there you have it — the first successful action against the President of the United States during his horrific second term. The fight had come not from supposed opposition leaders in Washington, but from Burbank’s grassroots. People talk about Kimmel’s defense as the turning point in the second Trump presidency. (And for me, two wins. Something was changing.) Anti-ICE organizing All the while, ICE fascism terrorized our communities. I volunteered with the local rapid response network, building a social following by reporting on their movements. The cruelty was astonishing — a raid at the Children’s Refugee Center during a food drive remains the low point — and people started reaching out to me to ask how they could get involved. The organizing moves I had been making for a decade went from earning a few dozen reactions to tens of thousands. Know-Your-Rights clinics and workshops were full, anti-ICE patrols circulated daily, and ICE abductions were met with a furious public within minutes. I’ve spent my adulthood trying to get people to care about the things that I care about, but caring is tough when self-preservation comes at the cost of isolation. But the naked depravity of the second Trump presidency roused a critical mass of people into collective action. People reclaimed some of their power and directed it to the defense of their communities and themselves. In the middle of that surge of energy, I pulled the trigger on my ’26 campaign. There were three seats being contested, and one of the incumbents chose not to run. I felt like a frontrunner immediately — I had the institutional support that I lacked in the previous campaign, along with two straight years of constant public engagement. I knew the grassroots support was there for me, but I was in for a surprise: a second candidate had been drafted from the grassroots and put up for council. The Burbank Tenants Union had asked DSA organizer Nolan Southerland to run. I, Mr. Routine Loser, immediately couched it in familiar terms: “I hope you win and I certainly think you can, but it’s a late entry. You may not get the institutional support you need, and we’re up against some amoral conservatives that will doubtlessly drown us in dark money. Do you have a plan for a loss?” I expected my extraordinarily long, bumpy ride to happen to most potential candidates regardless of how impressive they were. Surely, a first-timer like Nolan had the odds stacked against him, and I needed to focus on my own race. I wanted to hope for a best-case scenario of a clean sweep, but I’d lost so many times in the run-up to this moment. On Election Day, I braced for mixed news. The Burbank grassroots The grassroots powered this win It wasn’t Nolan I’d underestimated, or even myself. It was the grassroots — the progressive movement writ large. Somewhere between 20 to 40 volunteers showed up every week to knock thousands of doors. I’d knocked 7,600 over two campaigns, and I’d carried more than my own literature at every opportunity for a group canvass. My decade of losses had added up to a commanding (second-place) victory, and the limitless energy of the Burbank grassroots movement reelected terrific progressive Nikki Perez and created a one-and-done democratic socialist victor in Nolan Southerland. People wanted change, and Burbank picked three changemakers. After my first loss in 2017, I wrote a consolation speech called “When We Win”: When we win, we will win harder and more absolutely than any fake, troll, billionaire president or sellout establishment hack can imagine. When we win, we will have student loan debt forgiveness and give the primes of our students’ lives back to them. When we win, we will have a single-payer healthcare system that guarantees treatment regardless of income. When we win, we will have an economy that says no matter if you rent or own a home, everybody deserves to have enough income to live with dignity, save for the future, and contribute to their communities. When we win, we save this planet from the horrors of an economy built solely for today’s profit over tomorrow’s well-being. Call it a list of demands. So here I am with an uplifting identity crisis: a loser, a proud loser, having won , staring down the size of the responsibility we have as the modern era’s first socialist city council. The work isn’t done, not by a long shot — we need to deliver to prove that progressives can govern effectively. Mamdani has set the pace and we need to keep it. So I can no longer lose. That part of my life is over. But this challenge is mirrored in the progressive movement: We can no longer lose. And we will no longer lose. The inflection point is behind us, and from now on our consistency will go in favor of victory, because we’ve shown each other — we’ve shown ourselves — that despite failure upon failure, nothing stops us. Whether we took a long road or a short one, we’ve arrived . Now, we link arms and move forward. * California Red is researching the question of first-ever DSA City Council majority. It may well be true. But there were at least three DSA members on the seven-member Santa Cruz City Council in the 1980s, including mayor Mike Rotkin. If there was a fourth that body would claim to have been the first. If you know the answer, contact California Red editor Fred Glass ( fglasscft@gmail.com ).

articles.title: The Revolutionary Cocktail: Why DSA Needs Electoralism, Direct Action, and Mutual Aid to Win
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: PART TWO OF TWO [Part One appeared in the September issue of California Red . Here it is.] Now, there was an invisible through line in all three of the examples of local direct action— and that is mutual aid. When I was a ‘baby leftist,’ developing my sea legs, organizing with the PSL, mutual aid was cast aside as functionally useless anarchist praxis. It was considered band-aids for bullet holes, I was told. However, when I was cutting my teeth during the Student Intifada, organizing alongside Dutch anarchists at the University of Amsterdam, the mutual aid component to the encampments was unavoidable. In fact, it was practically baked into the whole concept! If we wanted to sustain an encampment or occupation, we simply needed supply lines that could feed and water the several hundred students, staff, and faculty demanding the university divest from Israel. This got me thinking; if we were serious about revolutionizing society, did that merely entail commandeering existing supply chains, hitting the Teamsters and Longshoremen with a coat of red paint, prefixing big chain supermarkets with “The People’s Grocery Outlet,” and calling it a day? Urban versus Rural I sat with this thought. In the midst of encampments and occupations, I was also finishing up my masters thesis on the way that geographic conditions shape organizing strategies; examining the differences and similarities of urban versus rural approaches to radical politics. A core pillar of the thesis was exposing the extractive relationship between cities and the countryside as being a microcosm of the relationships perpetuated by capitalist-colonialism, i.e., between imperial cores and their peripheries. The relations of production and distribution are inseparable from the mode of production in which they exist. That might seem abundantly apparent at a theoretical level, but the implications for local organizing are tremendous. Obviously, we want logistics and grocery workers to have strong protections and safe working conditions, where they make good money for the work they contribute to maintaining our supply chains. But simply putting these logistics networks under control of the workers won't change the fact that rural communities suffer from severe underdevelopment and precarious access to goods and services, and it certainly won't fix the “noble savage” view of urban dwellers against their rural counterparts. I’ll be the first to say that DSA won't be the organization that fixes this structural imbalance in the supply chain or be the mechanic to the relationship between urban and rural communities. That is a longterm problem that will require a serious overhaul in how we shape production and distribution both at home and abroad (good thing we are an anti-imperialist socialist organization!). However, what I want to emphasize here is that the projects and campaigns being worked on by DSA San Diego’s Ecosocialist working group and our mutual aid collective are not simply acts of kindhearted charity but deeply rooted in a theory of building sustainable community power. Seeding Food Sovereignty is an active campaign by EcoSoc that prioritizes building out community gardens throughout the city that can supplement the caloric intake of the local community. The organizational concept is that by proliferating community garden infrastructure, urban and especially suburban communities can reduce their dependence on alienated supply chains that function to obfuscate where their produce originates. Rather than an intermediary of fluorescent lighting and underpaid service workers, our gardens are sites of community building over the labor it takes to feed one another. The program functions on the old Marxian adage “from each according to their ability, to each according to their needs.” It’s no secret that gardening can be back-breaking work, but the organizers of each garden workday take each person's ability into account by offering a variety of tasks scaled by intensity. From pulling weeds and picking fruit to digging up tree stumps and building planters, there is always something for everybody. Noble charity? The event “Race the 215” advocated for public transportation support. The cyclists (shown prepping here) won the race when the bus broke down. Too often, I see criticisms of mutual aid endeavors made in the same tone with which my PSL comrades once castigated it to me: mutual aid is just noble charity which doesn't really turn the dial forward in terms of growing organizational power and is ultimately futile in the face of deeply inequitable and imperial supply chains. However, it is important to understand that the motivation behind this campaign is not to merely patch gaps in the system of distribution. Nor will mutual aid ever be able to outright replace a deeply embedded and globalized supply chain. Rather, the purpose of mutual aid such as these gardens is to cohere a community of individuals around the physical labor of building infrastructure that supports a community’s basic needs. This is an integral aspect of building a meaningful socialist project that proves we have the vision, means, and ability to build novel production and distribution structures that do not perpetuate capitalist-colonialist relations and are organized in common rather than at the direction of capital. Another similarly effective mutual aid project of the San Diego chapter is our Fix the 215 campaign. The 215 is a local bus line with the highest ridership in the city; beginning at the train station in downtown and terminating at the local state university, it takes about 50 minutes from start to finish for a total of nine miles (and that is if the bus does not break down midway through). Our demands were quite simple: dedicated bus lanes, all door boarding, and bus priority at intersections. The most recent action related to this project was Race the 215, where we partnered with our cyclist and urbanist advocacy partners to facilitate a competition between bicycle riders and the 215 bus line to see which group could finish the route faster. Needless to say, the cyclists won after the bus broke down three stops into the race. The event itself had a tinge of direct action blended into it, but the project of public transportation advocacy more broadly demonstrates a priority for reinforcing and expanding an existing working class community infrastructure that is centered around accessibility and the freedom of movement. A project such as this, however, will not be completed simply on its merits alone, and we are under no illusions that, by merely documenting significant flaws in the public transportation system and advocating for meaningful solutions, these issues will ever be fixed. We will need buy-in from the elected officials that sit on the governing authority for public transportation, the San Diego Association of Governments (SANDAG), a multi member body made up of elected officials from the City and County of San Diego as well as various periphery cities. A sustainable socialist project At the end of the day, we are in the business of politics. That means running candidates, raising money, and winning races. It is unmistakable that DSA is in the shape that it is because we have proven ourselves to be a viable alternative to decades of austerity at the ballot box. But as our comrades in any of the various groupuscules and sectariana will always remind us, the road to electoral victory is paved with opportunists and reformism. Is simply changing the flag flown at city hall to a red rosy handshake actually building a sustainable socialist project? Working people obviously lead busy lives and mundane political engagement is taxing enough, let alone organizing. Yet, through an Electoralist strategy, reforms can be fought for and won in local institutions that can alleviate some of the burden of our neoliberal hell while also demonstrating the upper ceiling of capitalist reforms (centering this concept in messaging is crucial; there will always be a box that needs breaking out of). Putting your comrade Fran or Ken in charge of the state is only the starter gun for change at the structural level. Once in office, passing policy becomes the flipside of Electoralism that can really make or break its efficacy as a grand strategy. And if the executors of the administrative bureaucracy cannot impose the will of the masses on captured political structures, then those structures prove why they must be altered or abolished. Zohran is not a good mayor because he agrees with me and is the same type of communist as I am: he is a good mayor because he actually uses his position to advance and entrench the interests of his constituents at large. Taking power where we can, then wielding it accordingly is truly the base spirit of this whole cocktail. The point of engaging in Electoralism is not about taking power for power's sake, it is in order to soften material conditions so that the most politically advanced of the masses can build a holistic movement that includes the work of direct action against defenders of the capitalist order and building the dual power infrastructures that will eventually render the state obsolete. When all three happen at the same time, that is prefiguring. This will occur most literally at the hyper-local level; i.e. organizing a residential building to lower their rent by forming a tenant union and passing a local rent control ordinance through an allied alderperson. Through participation in that struggle, those tenants will have lower rents, giving them more free time, while simultaneously demonstrating that DSA is people who get shit done– and that is better recruitment and development than any list someone could whip up. A constructive tension Electoralism also serves as a test of reach and effect. The worst outcome of a solely Direct Action and/or Mutual Aid strategy is organizing oneself into a bubble that is alienated from the masses at large. For better or for worse, ~150m Americans believe that voting is the ultimate form of political participation. If our work is resonating with communities, that should be reflected in every single primary and general election. Voting maps and district research become data points for targeted outreach strategies in support of mutual aid projects that aim to serve communities before, during, and after election day. Getting these projects started early and in election off years demonstrates to a community that DSA is not Johnny Come Latelys, but that we come from and have deep bonds to the communities we wish to represent. Another holistic aspect to Electoralism is directly related to the attitude of the administrative and elected personnel of the government apparatus who manage the relations of production under which Direct Action and Mutual Aid efforts play out. These electeds can swing favors significantly for grassroots infrastructure initiatives and allow for closer coordination with allied power brokers in negotiations. Even allied elected officials, by nature of their position to the capitalist mode of production, will naturally be restrained by the rigidity of the system, and thus must rely on their organized base to agitate for more concessions from the ruling class and deeper structural reforms. If the state is not capable of satisfying community interests, then its resources can be leveraged to build novel community-based institutions by and for the people. DSA San Diego, despite our size, is still building up our electoral program and is currently vying for the mayorship in two distinct periphery cities within the county. Each presents unique conditions in the project of building socialism and exciting opportunities for changing the dynamic between citizens and the city, easing the financial burden of existence, and creating novel infrastructure that supports working class liberation. Being in a democratic organization, politics plays out at every level–from chapter organizational priorities to who we endorse for public office. As we build our electoral muscles, the team sports tradition so thoroughly embedded in American politics manifests as an internal tension between two camps: the chapter institutionalists, intent on building a sustainable political machine, and the political firebrands, who see winnable seats as platforms to agitate and disrupt business as usual. I want to emphasize that I find this tension to be a constructive one. Watching the various camps emerge just within the ecosystem of electoralism has exposed natural leaders and demanded their creativity in deploying organizing tactics that can win the support of chapter membership. The institutionalists remind us that power requires endurance— you can't govern if you can't win. The firebrands, on the other hand, remind us that winning is meaningless if you do not use the platform to build movement power and shift the terms of debate. Both are necessary, as the dialectic of building and agitating plays out in real time. Only time will tell if our comrades ascend to their respective Mayoralties, but, at the very least, the chapter will have gained ambitious new leaders and experienced structural innovation that builds a culture of excitement and progress. In the end, the left movement in the US is ultimately in a period of strategic fermentation, maturing into the grownup world of congressional primaries and talking head interviews, while trying to maintain an optimistic vision of what a socialist future can be if only we can win the moment in the now. Through a balanced synthesis of these three tactics, the revolutionary cocktail is brewed, but only if united by a holistic strategy that balances the strengths and weaknesses of each component of the concoction. Our task is not to predetermine the lines of development, but to embrace the unity of our work and the necessity of that unity for the most thorough advance of our movement. Without tapping into the essence of elections, mutual aid, and direct action–each of them loses the potency to be genuinely revolutionary. I'll leave you with this axiom. If an industry or institution for a service exists, then you unionize it through direct action or capture it electorally; and if the structure does not yet exist, then you build it through mutual aid. [Reprinted from Geese ]

articles.content: CalSTRS (California State Teachers’ Retirement System) is the world’s largest educator-only public pension fund, delivering reliable returns to investors while managing billions of dollars of assets.
