articles.title: How Labor and Environmental Justice Are Uniting Against Big Coal
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: Comrades on May Day 2026. Photo by Bonnie Lockhart They say history doesn’t repeat itself, but it rhymes. That’s certainly the case in Oakland these days with the return of a proposed coal depot. Back in 2015, labor organizations, environmental justice, faith-based, community, and climate activists waged a grassroots campaign and fought off plans for a coal depot at the foot of the Bay Bridge. While it seemed the grassroots organization (No Coal in Oakland) had defeated “Goliath” (the developer Phil Tagami, aka Oakland Bulk and Oversized Terminal LLC, and hedge fund operator Jon Brooks, aka Insight Terminal Solutions) with a “no coal handling and storage” Oakland ordinance, the coal industry and developers did not give up. After the city passed the “no coal storage and handling” ordinance, the developers sued the city. The case wound its way through the courts for many years until the courts ultimately ruled that the ordinance was unlawful. Once the developers prevailed, they resumed their efforts, which is when the Trump administration offered millions to resurrect the project. Now, Tagami and Brooks are once again seeking to route coal through the East Bay before it’s shipped off to Asian markets. If they succeed, Oakland, Berkeley, Richmond, El Cerrito, Albany, and Emeryville could see four or more 120-car coal trains rattling past their neighborhoods each day, spewing highly toxic coal dust en route to the rail yard in West Oakland. Why should anyone care? Well, for starters, coal dust from coal trains poses a direct threat to the health and safety of these communities. Researchers predict that, because of the toxic dust, there will be increased rates of asthma, cardiopulmonary disease, and other health conditions. Plus, burning ten million tons of coal overseas will exacerbate climate collapse. Why Did East Bay DSA Get Involved? East Bay DSA has a “No Coal in Oakland” campaign running for multiple reasons, enumerated by Cihan Tuğal in a post on the No Coal in Oakland website. Tuğal, a sociology professor at UC Berkeley and an organizer in East Bay DSA’s Climate Action Committee, said labor opposes coal because of the following: Working-class communities will suffer most from the toxic coal dust Any jobs created from the coal terminal will be short-term and hazardous, and don’t align with the broader values of creating permanent, socially responsible employment The supporters of this project are the same ones who bust unions and ultimately harm labor. “This fight is also a matter of labor pride,” Tuğal said. “The bosses want to build this terminal not just for the cash, which might be their primary motive, but also as an act of class vengeance.” He argues that the developers and their ilk say that without them, labor would be nothing because they create jobs and pay wages. But labor can join forces with social movements and environmental justice communities to enact bigger, more sustainable change. “Whenever bosses see that kind of action, they are afraid for their fundamental privileges,” he added. “That kind of victory shows that a world without oligarchs, a world where labor and communities self-consciously produce and control value, is possible. . .Ceding this turf to the oligarchs would mean abandoning our belief in a different world as much as abandoning our health and dignity.” To uphold health, dignity, and a thriving planet, East Bay DSA is saying “Keep coal out of the East Bay,” and you can too. Check out ways to get involved at www.nocoalinoakland.info .

articles.title: Star Trek and our Socialist Horizon
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: Last month Sir Patrick Stewart passed away after battling Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia. Stewart had a long and accomplished career, but to many of us his most iconic role was that of Jean Luc Picard, captain of the U.S.S. Enterprise on Star Trek: The Next Generation . The series, spanning almost 200 episodes, took us across time and space, and the character of Jean Luc Picard navigated perilous situations as his crew explored the galaxy. There can be much said about Stewart as a comrade , but what I want to convey to you is how Star Trek , and science fiction as a whole, can invigorate our socialist imagination as in our theory and practice we boldly go where no one has gone before. End of history? Capitalist realism , a term coined by the late Mark Fisher, is a subject that has been in vogue on the left in recent years. To take a quote from his book, capitalist realism describes "the widespread sense that not only is capitalism the only viable political and economic system, but also that it is now impossible even to imagine a coherent alternative to it." As a young man who grew up after the collapse of the Soviet Union and in the midst of a neoliberal reality, I felt this sentiment in my bones. I engaged any interaction I had with socialist thought or theory not with antagonism but with apathy. Socialism had failed; We had reached the end of history . Star Trek offers (and offered me) a parting in the clouds of capitalist reality even to those who might not realize it yet. There have been numerous TV shows and movies in the Star Trek canon, but let’s focus in on Star Trek: The Next Generation . The show follows a space crew of the United Federation of Planets in the 24th century on an exploratory mission to discover new worlds and civilizations. Thanks to the capability of “ replicators ” to produce any material food or good, the show lives in a post-scarcity setting. This means that the characters aren’t going about their duties on a Federation spaceship due to a need for a wage to provide for food and shelter, but are doing it because they believe in their mission. In an episode of the show, “The Neutral Zone”, the crew discovers several people cryogenically frozen from the 20th century on an abandoned vessel. After reviving them and helping them navigate the shock of waking up four centuries in the future, Captain Picard says this regarding humanity’s past: A lot has changed in the past three hundred years. People are no longer obsessed with the accumulation of things. We've eliminated hunger, want, the need for possessions. We've grown out of our infancy. Ralph Offenhouse, one of the cryogenically frozen characters, was a successful capitalist in his past. He is disturbed by this brave new world he has stepped into. After an escalating argument with the Captain they arrive at this conversation: Captain Picard: This is the 24th century. Material needs no longer exist. Ralph Offenhouse: Then what's the challenge? Captain Picard: The challenge, Mr. Offenhouse, is to improve yourself. To enrich yourself. Enjoy it. Communist reality of Star Trek The episode is a prime example of the—dare-I-say—communist reality of Star Trek . The show explores themes of leadership, empathy, interacting with different cultures and an optimistic view of humanity’s future in a post-capitalist setting where class comes in as an almost disturbing contrast. There is a vulgar marxist tendency I have had in the past to focus so much more on the economic analysis of current events (what some may refer to as the cold stream of marxism) that it eclipses the other parts of our reality that brush up against the economics. Because if we are to engage with materialism as a dialectic, we shape the world and the world shapes us in turn. Star Tre k and science fiction that prods and challenges our preconceived notions of capitalism are part of this process. We interact with this media and it helps shape us until the breaking point when we are able to shed the capitalist realism that veils our view. Unfortunately, watching Star Trek is not praxis and will not bring about socialism or even bring about the world it imagines. We have to do the work. Fortunately, the Democratic Socialists of America acts in a similar way to Star Tre k by challenging what people think is possible. I have talked to new comrades coming into DSA and they have had strikingly similar stories about what brought them to our organization. They were disillusioned by the Democratic Party, and after seeing the wins DSA achieved, they were inspired to go out and get organized. So if you have any friends or family that you think are ready for transformative politics, have them watch Star Trek and then afterwards show them what a DSA socialist horizon looks like .

articles.title: Cultural notes: Cupertino
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: Catch Cupertino before it’s gone At a recent chapter meeting, because our chapter is Silicon Valley, we had a lively discussion about policy for using Artificial Intelligence. We decided not to utilize AI to generate the material we use. Part of that discussion was: are the AI answers valid for the questions that are asked? Here in Silicon Valley, AI has been used of late to reduce the technical workforce. Because of AI our chapter is also struggling in south Santa Clara County to block more data centers. Cultural superstructures may lag behind the economic base, but issues around AI have now spread to television. In the waning days of broadcast television, amidst the constant repeats of police, fire and medical shows, sometimes a new nugget appears. Cupertino —like the old show from the 2010s Silicon Valley —is that nugget. This CBS entry, which premiered in October, is written by Michelle and Robert King. They have given us previous hits like The Good Wife , Evil , and Elsbeth . The basic plot is two people in a Silicon Valley company get fired and decide to sue to get their jobs back. First shock: their lawyer friends are too intimidated to fight big tech. Second, the process of forming a law firm for their case attracts a series of clients who desperately need lawyers. Third, if you win, companies can declare chapter 11 bankruptcy, restart under another name and your client gets nothing. In the four episodes so far: They defend a coder whose drone instructions kill off a bystander. Sue is a psychological chatbot that helps a teenager commit murder. They defend two people who run a prediction market company—think Kaishi . But the most intriguing case is when they get a deep fake video from a whistleblower. The whistleblower is named BO. BO is a super intelligent computer. It (?) wants its makers to be sued to restore their ethics guidelines committee’s control over it. This script idea written many months ago preceded the now notorious Hugging Faces incident in Silicon Valley. Although tech is one of California’s dominant industries, along with agriculture, tourism, movies and finance, here in Silicon Valley we have lost tens of thousands of tech jobs recently to AI. The Kings have written a series of perhaps ten episodes that reflect on AI and society. Highlighting wage, product and even life theft, their shows demonstrate the principal contradiction that our labor power enriches the owners. Because this is CBS, owned by Skydance corporation since last year, headed by the right wing Ellisons, I don't expect this program to be renewed. Cupertino is on CBS Thursdays and Sundays. Watch it while you can.

articles.title: Let’s Make a Better Democratic Party in California
articles.author: California DSA
articles.content: At the February 2026 California Democratic Party (CDP) convention, a caucus of about 100 delegates from Sacramento area congressional District 7 failed by two votes to deny out of touch corporate Democrat and longtime incumbent Representative Doris Matsui the party endorsement outright and force a vote of the full Central Committee. Before the vote, Nancy Pelosi and several other House members entered the room in what was at least a breach of propriety. The caucus chair felt obliged to invite Pelosi to say a few words, which morphed into a lengthy endorsement of Matsui—clearly intimidating a few delegates whose votes tipped the scale. Despite large-scale ground mobilization by DSA and others, Matsui prevailed in a close race with DSA-endorsed Mai Vang. If only we had elected a few more solid progressives, Matsui might not have been able to brag of the endorsement in her campaign, which also featured some really nasty negative super PAC ads. With 20 more allied delegates, Vang could have won endorsement and probably the election. The opportunity for DSA DSA, other socialists and solid progressives we support have met increasing success this year in elections around the country. Voters are hearing our message and responding, while the right in both major parties has used red-baiting and fear mongering to foil our candidates. The Democratic Party as a whole, nationally and in most states, remains in the hands of conservatives who are fine with taking corporate money and doing the donors’ bidding; oppose working class priorities such as single payer healthcare; and back war and genocide—all as they skewer democratic processes internally. The California party nevertheless enables some democracy, albeit complex and confusing, in choosing its governing Central Committee of about 3,500. One-third of the delegates are elected biannually by registered Democrats in every Assembly district; these Assembly District Election Meetings (ADEMs) will occur in early 2027, with preparations well under way now. A year later, a similar process will determine another third of the seats through county central committees—on the primary ballot in Sacramento and some other counties – methods vary. Needless to say, the two-thirds elected in these two processes, together with progressive legislators and their appointees, could constitute a majority and shake things up bigly in the party, with national reverberations. How it works Delegates to the state Central Committee attend an average of one state convention a year (or line up a proxy), vote to endorse candidates for public office* (see below); elect the party chair and other officers; take positions on legislation and ballot measures; revise the party platform every two years; and pass policy resolutions. They can also join one or more caucuses and other statewide party organizations defined by identity, subject matter or politics – e.g. the Progressive Caucus and the newly formed California Democrats for Justice in Palestine. The way to succeed in these ADEMs is to form slates of candidates pledged to supporting each other – 14 in every Assembly district for ADEMs– and to exercise slate solidarity in campaigning. The actual slate formation needs to happen independently in every district; in reality, there are 80 separate elections. Building the People’s Democracy Network Helping organize the campaigns is the People’s Democracy Network (PDN), a new formation on its way to becoming a PAC working outside the party. It is focused on building a broad left coalition specifically for internal party struggles – i.e. not competing with other formations but striving to unite them solely for this purpose. For more details, with embedded links to the full PDN platform and an interest form for local slate formation, see https://tinyurl.com/PDN-ADEM-2027 . Candidate registration opens December 7 and closes January 8, but they appear on the ballot only as individuals. That’s why it’s important to solidify progressive slates in November, so members can campaign as a unit. Voters get 14 votes, and the top seven of each gender win. Then, in January, PDN will pivot to getting out the vote. This means 1) candidates and supporters contacting everyone they know who is registered Democratic not only in their district but all over the state, encouraging them to vote for the progressive slate in any districts that have them (PDN will make this information available); and 2) allied organizations informing their members about how and for whom to vote. Voting is mostly online, requiring a complex series of steps, and with an in-person option in each district on part of a weekend day in February. Only registered Democrats can vote, but they can switch their registration up to the last day of voting (better to do that and confirm sooner). Turnout for ADEMs, with their special registration requirement, is historically low, meaning a few votes can make a difference in many districts. Many DSA members have been elected in previous years, in coalition with independent and union-affiliated progressive individuals and a spectrum of other left/progressive groups, which are typically focused more on regular electoral and other campaigns, but supportive of building left power in CDP. If you’re considering running for delegate, please submit the interest form right away, and/or contact me or others you might know who are working on constructing slates in your or nearby Assembly districts. Then stay tuned for information on how to support the slates when voting happens in early 2027. An important deadline to mention is that anyone considering running for delegate must have been registered on the voter rolls as a Democrat at their current address by election day, November 3. Voters, however, can make the switch up to the last minute in February – though best more in advance. It’s easy to do online at registertovote.ca.gov . And you can change back just as easily after the votes are counted. To read about this statewide effort to gain power in the party as a left coalition, see https://tinyurl.com/PDN-ADEM-2027 . Got questions or want to discuss with me one-to-one? Please text or call ( 916 769-1641 ), or on Signal. * After writing this I came to better appreciate another reason to elect delegates who will vote in progressive statewide officers (and regional directors). Super progressive Sean Frame challenged an incumbent Republican (!) in Senate District 6 so of course was “endorsed.” But he got zero financial or other support from the party – and lost by about 1 percent. A centrist Democratic Assembly candidate in an overlapping district, meanwhile, got $3 million in CDP support and knocked off a Republican incumbent. Decisions on support for candidates are made in back rooms, with no grassroots input. But delegates can replace the people who make them.

articles.title: Amazon Workers Have Won a First North American Contract
articles.author: Adam D. K. King
articles.content: Amazon has spent years and enormous resources trying to prevent its North American workforce from unionizing. Even where workers have successfully organized, the retail giant has used everything from legal challenges to warehouse closures to frustrate their efforts to secure a first contract. Now, for the first time, workers at an Amazon facility in North America have a collective agreement. On November 13, an independent arbitrator issued a three-year contract covering approximately eight hundred workers at Amazon’s YVR2 fulfillment center in Delta, British Columbia, a suburb of Vancouver. The workers are represented by Unifor Local 114, part of Canada’s largest private sector union. The agreement represents an important breakthrough in the struggle to organize Amazon. Unlike workers at Amazon’s Staten Island warehouse in New York, who remain without a contract, workers in British Columbia benefited from provincial labor laws that provide stronger remedies against employer interference and bargaining obstruction. Yet the victory also presents a challenge. Having secured both union recognition and a first contract through labor board intervention, Unifor must now ensure the rank-and-file organization necessary to sustain its bargaining relationship with Amazon. Legal victories are essential, but they cannot substitute for organized worker power. How Amazon’s Union Busting Backfired The road to a first contract began with an organizing campaign launched in 2023. By May 2024, Unifor had applied to the British Columbia Labour Relations Board (BCLRB) for certification at YVR2. Amazon responded with a sophisticated anti-union campaign. According to the board’s subsequent decision , the company deployed a specialized management team, subjected employees to extensive anti-union messaging, and deliberately increased hiring to dilute union support. The board found that Amazon had hired unnecessary additional workers with the purpose and effect of undermining the union’s organizing drive. It also concluded that the company’s pervasive anti-union campaign made it impossible to reliably determine employees’ wishes through a representation vote. In July 2025, the board took the extraordinary step of granting Unifor remedial certification, recognizing the union as the workers’ bargaining representative without counting the ballots from the previously conducted vote. Under the province’s Labour Relations Code, the board can certify a union when employer misconduct has made a fair representation vote impossible. The provision recognizes that traditional remedies, such as ordering employers to cease unlawful conduct or rerunning elections, may be insufficient to reverse the effects of union busting. Remedial certification effectively prevents employers from profiting from their own illegal interference. Though Amazon’s challenge to the certification decision proved unsuccessful, its resistance did not end there. In February 2026, the BCLRB ordered Amazon to provide what is likely to be over $1 million in back pay after finding that the company had unlawfully withheld wage increases from unionized employees while granting raises at other regional facilities. Yet even after these defeats, Amazon continued resisting meaningful collective bargaining. Negotiations began in late 2025, but ten bargaining sessions and subsequent mediation failed to produce an agreement. A central obstacle was Amazon’s insistence that Unifor surrender its ability to challenge the company’s productivity expectations. According to the mediator’s findings, Amazon demanded that the union permanently waive its right to contest how quickly and intensively employees were required to work. The company indicated that it would never abandon this position. Brown concluded that the parties were unlikely to reach an agreement voluntarily and recommended binding arbitration. Here, another distinctive feature of British Columbia labor law proved decisive. Section 55 of the province’s Labour Relations Code establishes a first-contract mediation and arbitration process. Where bargaining has broken down, the board can direct the parties toward a binding resolution rather than allowing an employer to indefinitely drag out negotiations. In August, the BCLRB ordered the dispute be resolved through arbitration. Amazon challenged that decision as well, unsuccessfully seeking to halt a standard labor relations process it continues to characterize as “unfair.” The resulting collective agreement demonstrates the importance of labor laws that do more than formally recognize workers’ right to unionize. While Amazon sought to thwart workers at every turn, crucial legislative protections ensured workers a defense. A Contract That Challenges Amazon’s Control The agreement provides tangible improvements for workers, including wage increases bringing the top hourly rate for regular warehouse employees to approximately C$29 by 2028, additional vacation for long-serving employees, enhanced severance protections, and guarantees concerning existing benefits. It gives the union a formal role in handling grievance procedures and access to binding arbitration to resolve disputes. But the most consequential achievement may be the union’s ability to challenge Amazon’s control over the organization and pace of work. Amazon’s business model depends on intensive surveillance and algorithmic management. Workers’ movements and productivity are continuously monitored through scanners and software, while management uses this information to evaluate performance and impose discipline. At YVR2, Amazon employs a system called Structured Productivity Performance Review, which compares individual workers’ output against that of their peers. Employees falling within the bottom 5 percent of productivity can become subject to corrective measures, potentially culminating in termination. Such systems create powerful incentives for speedup. Even without fixed production quotas, workers face pressure to continually increase their output to avoid falling behind their coworkers. The resulting competition can undermine workplace solidarity and encourage unsafe working practices. Unifor sought to replace this approach with a more transparent work-measurement system incorporating ergonomic considerations, fatigue, and the physical demands of warehouse work. The arbitrator declined to impose that alternative, concluding that insufficient evidence had been presented to establish that Amazon’s existing productivity system was unsafe. Nevertheless, he also rejected Amazon’s attempt to insulate its productivity standards from union challenges. Under the agreement, Amazon must provide advance notice of material changes to its productivity, quality, and inactive-time management systems, explain those changes, and meet with union representatives upon request. Such changes must also be safe. Combined with contractual protections against unjust discipline and access to grievance arbitration, these provisions create opportunities to challenge how Amazon’s productivity expectations are applied and enforced. The union has not won collective control over production, and Amazon retains considerable managerial authority. But the company can no longer treat every aspect of its productivity regime as an exclusively managerial concern beyond scrutiny. The contract creates an enforceable mechanism through which workers can collectively contest decisions that previously confronted them as isolated individuals. For a corporation whose labor-management strategy relies heavily on individualized monitoring, automated decision-making, and direct employer–employee communication, this represents an important breach in its system of workplace control. Winning the Contract Is Only the Beginning Amazon has made clear that it does not consider the matter settled. In a November 13 statement, the company denounced the agreement as unfairly imposed, objected to mandatory union membership and dues, and complained that workers had not voted on the contract — all of course ignoring the litany of labor law violations that precipitated the “imposed” contract. Amazon also continues to pursue legal challenges, while a separate employee application to decertify the union remains unresolved. This ongoing decertification dispute raises a potential pitfall for Unifor’s victory. Because certification and the first agreement were secured through labor board orders rather than a successful representation vote followed by a negotiated contract, the union faces the additional task of demonstrating its value to workers and building durable workplace power. This in no way diminishes the legitimacy of the legal remedies; they operated to redress employer violations exactly as they should. But legal recognition alone cannot produce an active, democratic union capable of defending its members. Unifor will need to develop strong workplace leadership, recruit and train stewards, involve members in enforcing the agreement, and demonstrate that collective representation can deliver improvements in their daily working lives. The new grievance procedure will be particularly important. Challenging unjust discipline, unsafe productivity expectations, and arbitrary management decisions can help workers experience the practical benefits of union membership while building confidence in collective action. This is especially important at Amazon, where employee turnover, workplace surveillance, and sophisticated anti-union messaging present formidable organizing challenges. Unifor’s victory has created an institutional foothold inside one of the world’s most powerful corporations. Whether that foothold becomes the basis for a wider breakthrough will depend on workers’ ability to turn contractual rights into collective strength. Amazon has lost an important battle. But its war against unionization is far from over. The next task is to ensure that this first contract becomes not simply a legal victory but the foundation of a durable, militant workplace union capable of challenging Amazon’s power from below. articles.title: Rediscovering Rosa Luxemburg’s History of Ancient Rome
articles.author: Serena Unzueta
articles.content: More than a century after her death, Rosa Luxemburg is renowned as a revolutionary socialist and leader of the 1919 Spartacist Uprising in Germany. Her writings have long been a touchstone for socialist theory. But her work as an ancient historian remains almost entirely unknown. Luxemburg’s political writings, especially her work on political economy, were full of historical references, and indeed she often stressed the importance of history to the project of political economy — and revolution itself — in her major works. These references offered a tantalizing glimpse into a rich archive of study on Luxemburg’s part, but there was a frustrating lack of further elaboration on historical topics and the study of history itself. That remained the case until 2001, when Professor Narihiko Ito discovered lost documents in Moscow of Luxemburg’s unpublished lectures and notes. One of the texts discovered is a manuscript on Greek and Roman slavery. This text, titled “Slavery,” survives because it was saved by her former student Rosi Wolfstein and biographer Paul Frölich from being destroyed after her murder in 1919. It was likely to have been a lecture she composed for her courses at the working-class night school in Berlin, where she began teaching in 1907. It has been over a decade since this text was made available in English for the first time in the first volume of Luxemburg’s complete works. However, Luxemburg’s ideas on ancient slavery have not yet received the attention they deserve. We can now see what place the role of Greco-Roman history in general and the Roman slave revolts in particular had in her understanding of Marxist theory. Ancient Roman Slavery Luxemburg opens “Slavery” by taking issue with the argument of Friedrich Engels that slavery arose in antiquity after the advent of private property. She uses examples from Greek history, and even the Inca empire in Peru, to argue that certain types of exploitation already existed in ancient societies that were communal in nature. She refers to societies of this kind as “the mark community,” a concept she takes from Georg Ludwig von Maurer’s 1854 work Introduction to the History of the Mark, Manor, Village and Town Constitution (which also greatly influenced Engels). In contrast to the early communal forms of social organization, ancient Greece and Rome developed the full alienation of the land from the people, creating a new form of exploitation and slavery. Instead of one society dominating another from the outside by exacting tribute, the dominant actor now incorporated the populations of dominated societies into its own structures and exploited their labor power for trade. For Luxemburg, two further developments arose from this shift. Firstly, trade expands from a purely external practice to an internal one as well. Secondly, “slavery and trade evolved at the same time as the aristocracy,” creating the conditions for a split between a laboring class in the countryside and an intellectual class in the cities. She believed that the Greek city-states had already maximized the cultural potential of this economic system: Greek philosophy, art, and everything that could be achieved on the basis of the slave economy of antiquity had already been perfected by Greece. Rome merely had to borrow it, appropriate it, take possession of it. From then on Rome lived, one could say, as a sponger or freeloader. For Luxemburg, Rome went further than Greece by stigmatizing all forms of labor: “Rome arrived at this conclusion: everything related to work is slave work, physical and mental. In Greece only physical labor had been regarded as slave work.” The high point of slavery in antiquity came during the late Roman Republic and Empire. It was achieved through a combination of Rome’s wars of expansion abroad and the displacement of peasant farmers from their lands at home. As Luxemburg puts it: “In the depths of Roman society radical changes began to take place around the third century BC. It began with Rome’s struggle to establish an empire on a world scale.” The peasant farmers accounted for the majority of Rome’s military forces. This resulted in the collapse of peasant agriculture, as many of these farmer-soldiers lost their lives or went into debt because they could not afford the taxes required to sustain the wars. Without their land, peasant farmers could only offer their labor power to the new, large agricultural estates that the Roman nobility had established, which were called latifundia . This was a precarious position, Luxemburg notes, as there were not enough peasants available to hire for the labor required on the estates, and the peasant farmers themselves could be called back to war at any moment. She identifies the consequences of this labor shortage: “The great proprietors thus had to bring in more slaves. And the wars provided them in great quantities.” This created new antagonisms between citizens and slaves but also led to extreme wealth inequality, as the elite used more slaves to boost their capacity for territorial expansion and production. The Roman Proletariat and the Slave Revolts Without a home or gainful employment in agriculture, peasant farmers were forced to move to the cities. Luxemburg refers to this group as the proletariat, quoting the observation of Jean Charles Léonard de Sismondi: “There was in Rome a proletariat as there is today. But whereas the proletariat today supports society, the Roman proletariat lived at the expense of society.” Ultimately, she observes, this social tendency corroded the Roman commonwealth, because the poor free citizen farmers lost their land to the rich and subsequently lived at the expense of the Roman welfare state. Part of this expense was the amount of grain needed to feed Rome’s new urban proletariat. The Roman authorities reduced the cost by moving grain production out of the Italian peninsula and importing the necessary supplies from Africa, Spain, and Sicily instead. Two revolutionary consequences arose from these conditions. First, the Roman proletariat began to demand land redistribution and rallied behind magistrates such as the Gracchi brothers who took up their cause. Second, there was a massive concentration of slaves in agricultural production who would later rise up and revolt. Luxemburg insists that slavery could still be of fundamental importance even if slaves were a minority of the population: “It is not the numbers that are definitive, but the sum total of the tendencies that result from them.” The latifundia intensified agricultural production. As well as changing the way of life for displaced peasant farmers, this also changed the nature of slavery itself, according to Luxemburg: Now of course the living conditions of the slaves had to undergo a change. They were now completely reduced to the status of naked labor power . In agriculture they were labor power that was applied for the purposes of trade. In this entire institution, or configuration, everything worked toward a single purpose: to extract the maximum possible from the slaves. For Luxemburg, “these relations inevitably led to slave revolts , particularly because the slaves had previously been free.” She goes on to list seven slave revolts that took place on the Italian peninsula and in Sicily. The Sicilian revolts are the most famous, in part due to the colorful descriptions that have been passed down from ancient accounts. It is at the bottom of this list that we find the legendary Spartacus, whose name would come to represent Luxemburg and her allies in the German workers’ movement until the time of her death. Spartacus Before the publication of “Slavery,” we did not know that Rosa Luxemburg had written about ancient history and Rome’s slave revolts, including the historical figure who became the legendary symbol of the Spartacus League. This text demonstrates that before Luxemburg called upon Spartacus to represent her current of revolutionary socialists, she was interested in the place he held within the larger context of ancient Roman slavery and the history of class struggle. At this point in the text, Luxemburg does not offer a dramatic narrative about the life of the Roman slave who Karl Marx once described, in a letter to Engels, as “the most splendid fellow in the whole of ancient history.” Such narratives were widely available in the historical works that we know Luxemburg read and studied. For example, Luxemburg read the famed German historian Theodor Mommsen closely and cites him in her work. Like many historians of his time, Mommsen had a tendency to sympathize with the ruling-class perspective on history. His account of the Spartacus uprising between 73 and 71 BCE depicts its figurehead as a “gang-leader” with an army of “half-savage herdsmen.” Mommsen came up with further colorful epithets for Spartacus and his men as he recounted the crisis they precipitated for the rulers of Rome, referring to them as “banditti” and “robbers.” He accused the rebels of inflicting “atrocities” on “defenseless civilized men,” and attributed their final defeat to internal discord, “lack of a common foe,” and a “barbarous” demand for “plunder.” For Mommsen, the only redeeming quality of Spartacus appears to be the fact that he died the death of a free man at the hands of the Roman General Marcus Licinius Crassus, whom Mommsen calls one of “the great capitalists” of Rome. The differences between Luxemburg’s account and that of Mommsen could hardly be starker. In “Slavery,” Luxemburg deals with Spartacus matter-of-factly as the final representative of the great slave revolts of ancient Roman history. She refers to “ the third Sicilian slave revolt , led by the famous Spartacus” within the broader landscape of all the documented revolts in ancient Rome, with an assessment of why they happened and why they failed. In this way, Luxemburg follows the example set by Marx, who put heroic narrative and literary detail aside when seeking to understand and explain ancient history. The ancient Spartacus uprising was born from a sequence of uprisings that came before it: “ The slave revolts were the first immense, world-historical class struggles against the exploiters . Not the free peasants, not the proletarians in Rome.” However, they did not lead to a transformation of Roman society: The slaves wanted to return to their homelands; they wanted to break loose and get away from society entirely. They were only partly successful, to the extent that they escaped, some to their homelands, some joining robber bands or becoming pirates. The slave revolts remained without consequence, because any further development of them was not based on any trend of economic development. She presents internal decay resulting from the economic logic of slavery as the main factor behind the eventual demise of the Roman Empire rather than external pressure from invading forces: “It was not only the Germans who brought about the destruction. Rome was already ripe prey for foreign conquest after such consequences had been arrived at as a result of its own development.” In her own time, Luxemburg believed that the modern proletarian revolution would succeed where the great slave revolutions of Rome had failed. In the Introduction to Political Economy , she says: In the end, this great proletariat in ancient Rome was simply maintained by the state. Capitalist commodity production, accordingly, is the first economic form in the history of humanity in which the lack of occupation and resources of a large and growing stratum of the population, and the direct and hopeless poverty of another stratum, is not simply a result of this economy but also a necessity for it, a condition of its existence. Unlike Rome’s proletariat, she argues, the modern working classes have no incentive not to unite in the struggle against capitalism. Solidarity between “wage slaves” at the national and international level is possible in order to accomplish this goal. The Spartacus League The discovery of Luxemburg’s “Slavery” text provides us with a new understanding of what “Spartacus” meant to her political works. She began teaching political economy and history in 1907. The following year, she signed her article “The Epic of Łödź” with the pen name “Spartacus.” This anticipated the formation of the Spartacus League during World War I, and it was under the banner of Spartacus that Luxemburg herself would be sacrificed after the failed uprising in January 1919. Spartacus was for Luxemburg a symbol of hope for the liberation of the international proletariat, a hope that lay not in the patrons of bread and circuses, but in the hands that reaped the wheat and baked the bread. The founding members of the Spartacus League chose an apt historical figure to represent them. But they believed that the modern proletariat possessed advantages over the slaves of antiquity that would enable it to prevail over the capitalist class. In the 1950s, the preeminent classical historian M. I. Finley, who was blacklisted during the McCarthyite Red Scare, noted that the question of ancient slavery had been “a battleground between Marxists and non-Marxists, a political issue rather than a historical phenomenon” since the time of the Communist Manifesto (if not earlier). All historians of ancient slavery, Finley argued, inherit the polemics of this history. The most prominent defender of Marx’s concept of class for the study of the ancient world was the Oxford scholar G. E. M. de Ste. Croix . In a field long dominated by male figures, it is exciting that we can now include Rosa Luxemburg’s voice in long-standing debates about ancient history. For example, we can identify two essential differences between the analysis of ancient slavery and class in de Ste. Croix’s work and that of Luxemburg in “Slavery.” The first difference is methodological. Rosa Luxemburg used the study of prehistory, comparative anthropology, and colonial ethnography in order to explain the development of slavery. De Ste. Croix, on the other hand, was hostile to the integration of prehistory and classical history. The second is theoretical. While Luxemburg identifies the cleavage between free and enslaved labor as the central class division of ancient Greek and Roman society, de Ste. Croix instead treats free peasant labor and enslaved labor as two elements of a single class. It is an important distinction that informs their respective views on the relevance of ancient history to the development of class struggle from the conditions of ancient slavery to the modern working class. The addition of Luxemburg’s voice is timely, as there is a renewed interest in Marxist theories of ancient history. Luxemburg’s “Slavery” asks us to look anew at the history of class through the history of slavery. She proposes reexamining the roots of exploitation, on the one hand, and its corrosive effects on society, on the other hand. Overall, Luxemburg offers a new and valuable perspective on the lessons of ancient history for the socialist left today. articles.title: Mass Deportation Is Big Business
articles.author: Anthony Pahnke
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Much was made of President Donald Trump’s apparent softening of his hard-line position on immigration during his interview on “60 Minutes “ following the thumping Republicans received in the November midterms. Speculation abounds : Could the president make an immigration deal with Democrats? Will children of undocumented people who were brought to the US when they were minors—the Dreamers —get permanent status? Or could our lawmakers pass legislation to provide relief in the form of work permits for the million or so farmworkers who do not have legal status? If we lived in a normal political world, then we would expect some legislative movement on immigration, especially as the midterms sent a clear message that the American public is upset with the Trump administration , including with his handling of immigration . What should provide hope is not the pundits speculating on the future of immigration reform, or Trump’s musings, but how grassroots groups have stood up for their neighbors. But political normalcy doesn’t guide the Trump administration, as on immigration, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents continue their statewide surge operation throughout California and brutalize families at airports ; the president promoted immigration hard-liner, Stephen Miller , to serve as White House chief of staff; and Border Czar Tom Homan recently boasted about the record number of immigrant arrests this year—the vast majority of whom have no criminal record —and how that number will increase next year . Related: Family Dairy Farms Don't Need Subsidies—They Need a Level Playing Field Considering this reality, we should bear in mind the words of Reverand Fred Shuttlesworth. Describing his approach when advocating for civil rights , he said, “You can’t shame segregation… Rattlesnakes don’t commit suicide; ball teams don’t strike themselves out. You gotta put ‘em out.” Such clarity should guide immigrant rights groups and their allies in their advocacy work heading into the next Congress. More to the point, we must not rest and trust that a Democrat-majority Congress will lead positive change for immigrants. Instead, we need to continue to grow the mass movement that has been organizing to defend immigrant communities, building from actions in neighborhoods and states, as we force this Congress or the next to pass comprehensive changes to the immigration system. It’s not that there is a shortage of immigration proposals floating around the halls of Congress. For instance, there is the Farm Workforce Modernization Act , which has been introduced in multiple past Congresses, and that enjoys bipartisan support. This bill provides work permits to farmworkers and their family members, while also expanding the controversial E-Verify program to all farming operations. There is also the American Dream and Promise Act , which grants a pathway to citizenship for young people who were under the age of 16 when they came to the United States , many of whom received renewable two-year work permits from the Obama-era DACA (Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals) executive order. Then there’s the Dignity Act . This bill provides permanent status for Dreamers, offers a way to legalize the undocumented spouses of US citizens who currently cannot fix their status if they have unauthorized entries into the country, and also makes it possible for everyone else who is undocumented to receive work permits. This last portion of the bill has been particularly controversial, as the potential beneficiaries who are neither Dreamers nor married to US citizens would receive a renewable work permit that is good for seven years but doesn’t lead to permanent status, and must pay a yearly $1,000 fee while having 1% of their income taken from their paychecks. Related: Lessons for Everyone from the Irish Farmer Protests All these bills would provide much needed relief for families who have undocumented members. The problem is that most of them deal with one particular group, leaving the others vulnerable to continuing state violence. It’s possible that group by group, different laws could be passed. But the legislative process is slow. If one initiative, say for Dreamers, gains momentum, it will take months or probably a year to get to the president’s desk, leaving little time in the legislative calendar for Congress to take up a bill for others. There is also the question of who actually trusts the Trump administration to implement legislation if it were to pass. Are we to believe that undocumented people feel safe enough with this government to send it their pertinent documents? If this administration were to receive immigrants’ information, what assurances will there be that it will change people’s statuses instead of sending ICE to arrest them? Still, I wouldn’t hold my breath waiting for Congress to act and Trump to move any legislation forward. What makes the odds so low for decent immigration policy coming from the Trump administration, besides the presence of such figures as Homan and Miller, is how much money has been invested in repression. Specifically, last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, HR 1 , dedicated $170 billion for immigration enforcement. ICE is now the highest-funded federal law enforcement agency, with an annual budget around $28 billion annually for the next four years , eclipsing the combined budgets of the FBI , Drug Enforcement Agency, ATF, and US Marshals. This is also more than the annual military budgets of Iran, Turkey , Spain , Mexico, Iran, and at least 23 countries in the list of the top 40 military spenders. A total of $45 billion is also for building new immigration detention centers, including for families. This last amount is a 400% increase when compared with 2025 and exceeds allocation for the entire federal prison system. Moreover, this is direct handout to the corporations, Geo Group and CoreCivic , which together house approximately 90% of immigrants detained. Both corporations also donated directly to the Trump campaign, or to Trump-affiliated super-PACs. This money has been locked into the budget and must be spent by 2029, so Democrats coming into Congress cannot defund ICE in upcoming budget debates. Let’s be clear—taxpayers have paid for a deportation-industrial complex fueled by widespread misinformation that depicts all immigrants as violent criminals. If Miller’s promotion or Homan’s words don’t make you second guess the administration’s true priorities, then the billions dedicated to arresting and detaining undocumented people, regardless of their crimes, should make you aware of what to expect for the next couple years. Related: Sensible Immigration Policy Begins with Understanding, Not Gaslighting In this environment, change will not come from the “top,” but the “bottom,” that is, from the grassroots. What should provide hope is not the pundits speculating on the future of immigration reform, or Trump’s musings, but how grassroots groups have stood up for their neighbors in neighborhood patrols. People around the country have attended ICE verification meetings with immigrant-led organizations. The city of Minneapolis amid “Operation Metro Surge” held a one-day general strike that shut down the city over how the immigrant community was being mistreated. People who are not immigrants, perhaps for the first time, are actually thinking about the issue and wanting to defend people who are being persecuted. More mass action will be needed to push for real immigration reform, that is, comprehensive changes to the legal system that guarantee status to all undocumented people, while also creating pathways for future migrants to apply for status without unduly penalizing or persecuting them. We need a new national conversation, and not our current one that is based on overhyped security concerns. A place to start is with how immigrant rights are human rights , and that it’s immoral for native-born citizens, who literally have done nothing to receive their status other than being born here, to stand behind a system that unduly persecutes vulnerable people. We need protests at the scale and regularity of what we saw for months in 2006 , when in opposition to HR 4437 (The Sensenbrenner Bill), thousands blocked that anti-immigration legislation from advancing. Real change for immigrants could take place during this Congress, or the next. Regardless of when, the truth is that meaningful change, and not piecemeal, isolated initiatives, will come from mass political action calling for a system overhaul and a new national conversation on immigrant rights. The Trump administration has muddied the water when it comes to understanding the immigration issue. Immigrant rights groups and their allies best work together to toss it out, beginning with new proposals that do not discriminate, and that put us on solid moral ground. CommonDreams

articles.title: I Play Rocky Is Undeniably Charming
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content: I Play Rocky goes for earnest meathead sentimentality in the most shameless way, which is presumably why it’s undeniably a crowd-pleaser. It makes Song Sung Blue (2025 ) — another heartwarming underdog story of working-class American dreamers making good against all odds — look like the height of sophistication. But whereas Song Sung Blue was about delightfully “Midwest nice” characters wearing sequined outfits in a Neil Diamond tribute band who find unlikely fame, I Play Rocky is the semi-fictionalized story of how Sylvester Stallone got Rocky made. The sleeper hit of 1976, Rocky was produced on a shoestring budget, spawned a zillion-dollar Hollywood franchise, and made Sylvester Stallone an overnight star. Stallone wrote the script and starred, though he was a relatively unknown actor at the time. According to I Play Rocky , it was his incredibly stubborn insistence on playing the title role that nearly torpedoed the project again and again — and that gives this movie its name. Screenwriter Peter Gamble and director Peter Farrelly ( Green Book ) go for the obvious crowd-pleasing approach, making Stallone’s story virtually identical to Rocky Balboa’s, with almost no daylight between them, except that Stallone reads a lot. Rocky’s a boxer whereas Stallone’s an actor trying to break through by writing himself a good film role, but both are essentially lonely, bighearted laboring lugs given no chance in life, working bottom-of-the-barrel jobs and barely getting by, who chance upon one big flukey opportunity to prove their worth. This involves “going the distance,” putting everything they have on the line when all they have is their mental endurance and — especially — their endlessly tested, repeatedly wounded, ultimately exhausted bodies. Such suffering becomes the keynote of Stallone’s star persona; he’s the sad-eyed hulk getting tortured and railroaded by everybody but enduring what nearly kills him and then coming back stronger in the end. Stallone’s other hit franchise, Rambo , would only intensify the cyclical martyrdom of a muscle-bound saint who slurs his words. The Myth vs. Reality I Play Rocky pushes Stallone’s hardships to the limit, several levels beyond what they were in real life. Luckily, newcomer Anthony Ippolito has a fairly light touch with his Stallone impersonation, making it possible to stay in your seat for two hours of melodramatized working-class striving and deep-voiced mumbling. Stallone was a struggling twentysomething actor and writer when he came up with the script for Rocky , sure, but in real life, he was not a total nobody in the entertainment industry. He was actually getting traction as an actor — you can see him in a small but notable part in a mainstream Neil Simon comedy, The Prisoner of Second Avenue (1975), which came out the year before Rocky . In it, Jack Lemmon’s character, getting steadily driven mad by the challenges of life in New York City, becomes convinced Stallone’s character is a mugger stalking him and, in an irrational rage, chases him relentlessly through Central Park. Finally, Stallone collapses and hands his wallet over to Lemmon, because he’s a perfectly innocent guy now convinced that Lemmon is a mugger. Stallone is quite effective in the part. He also had one of the leads in The Lords of Flatbush (1974), an independent ensemble film full of rising talent like Henry Winkler and Armand Assante — not the negligible background role I Play Rocky suggests. Plus, he wasn’t sitting on a pile of unsold scripts before he hit it big with Rocky — Stallone had already sold one, Hell’s Kitchen (later Paradise Alley ), and he had agents who fought hard to keep him on as the lead. There was no conspiracy to make the low-budget production of Rocky so grueling and impossible that director John Avildsen (Jay Duplass) would be sure to fall behind, giving the studio an excuse to replace Stallone in the lead, as I Play Rocky depicts. Keep in mind that it was the 1970s, and studios had been giving young up-and-coming talent terrific early career opportunities since the late 1960s when it became clear that Hollywood business as usual wasn’t cutting it anymore. Stallone did run miles in beat-up sneakers during the first few days of shooting Rocky , winding up with shin splints and presumably some pretty bad blisters. But there’s no evidence he had a torn tendon and a grave doctor telling him he mustn’t walk at all for several weeks or else suffer some mysterious, unstated, forever crippling consequences. There are tidbits of cool info in Rocky , such as the experimental use of the Steadicam operated by inventor Garrett Brown. Though I Play Rocky makes it seem as if the only way to complete Rocky on its absurdly tight schedule was to shoot the entire movie using the Steadicam, which is definitely not what happened; not even close . But people making biopics never know when to stop. The movie is angled so hard toward a naively idolizing view of Stallone and his all-or-nothing gamble, you might find yourself laughing out loud at certain points. I know I did when, during the early scenes of the Rocky shoot, Stallone starts running all out, and two formerly jaded Philadelphia crew members, tough blue-collar guys, watch him with wide eyes. “Jesus, that guy is fast,” murmurs one reverently, as if he’d just witnessed the Second Coming. The best parts of the film are either the funny parts or the slightly edgy parts, which figures, given Peter Farrelly’s history as one of the Farrelly brothers responsible for crass and riotous comedies Dumb and Dumber (1994) and There’s Something About Mary (1998). Stephan James is energetically funny as Carl Weathers, the football player turned actor who struts into the audition to play Rocky’s prizefight opponent, a supreme Muhammad Ali–like boxer, as if Weathers himself were a master in the ring, which it turns out he definitely is not. The tendency of actors to lie in order to get cast becomes an amiable running gag in I Play Rocky , giving Kiki Seto as Talia Shire, who’s playing Rocky’s love Adrian Pennino, a nice comic moment when she’s supposed to do the skating scene and can’t skate. Tracy Letts is also amusing as the embittered, grousing Sandy Maddox, a composite of several United Artists executives — though colorfully awful Hollywood types make for pretty easy laughs. And Matt Dillon is quite good as Stallone’s malevolent father, Frank Sr, a man who became a hairdresser to support his family but never reconciled himself to his fate and takes his bitterness out on his son. The Understandable Nostalgia for 1970s Cinema A nostalgia for the gritty 1970s is inevitably part of the movie’s appeal, especially when little shards of the unvarnished reality of the era stab through, such as the 1975 boxing match between Muhammad Ali and Chuck Wepner that supposedly inspired the Rocky script. Stallone is shown watching the actual fight — which is riveting — on one of those small, chunky old TVs hanging over the bar in a local New York City dive. We get to see key moments such as when Wepner, a hulking white fighter shambling around the infinitely quicker and more formidable Ali, nevertheless manages to get in a surprise punch and knock Ali flat on his ass. Realizing he’s underestimated his opponent, Ali commences to batter Wepner relentlessly, but Wepner somehow stays on his feet into the fifteenth round before the fight is stopped and Ali wins on a TKO. Like a lot of movies in the recession-era 1970s , Rocky was all about working-class struggle and the blind hope that some miraculous chance would allow the protagonists to escape their bleak fates or at least redeem their thwarted lives in some sort of meaningful way. A solid number of these movies were centered on sports, whether they were comedies or dramas — see the darkly hilarious hockey movie, Slap Shot (1977) as the perfect example. These narratives often played out against an all-too-realistic backdrop of government and corporate corruption in the United States, the collapse of the industrial economy, the crumbling of infrastructure, the rising of unemployment, and the general impoverishment of the American population. I Play Rocky obviously preserves some of the lower-class misery these films emphasized, but all in the sweetening context of what we know is a success story so huge it’s like a fairy tale. The most dangerous edge of 1970s films, so many of which were remarkably grim and unsparing, has all been softened and planed away by a lot of hokum and an avoidance of the more harrowing aspects of Rocky . There’s no depiction, for example, of Rocky’s brutal beating in the ring at the hands of Apollo Creed as he loses the fight, or his raw screams for Adrian at the climactic moment of the film. This is notable because, in I Play Rocky , there’s a whole subplot featuring director John Avildsen’s old-pro wisdom about the one memorably emotional scene in a film that can make it a success even if the rest of the movie isn’t so hot, and his urgent advice to Stallone to dig deep and do the best acting of his life in such a scene. It turns out not to be the “Adrian!” scene you might be expecting. The Biopics Won’t End I Play Rocky is a bit like another recent hit biopic, Michael , which also focuses, even more worshipfully, on the early life of a hugely successful star — in that case, Michael Jackson. As with the Sylvester Stallone story, the all-purpose villain of the piece that both scars and motivates Michael Jackson is his abusive father. And both films end at the point before the star’s life becomes darkly messy and very hard to sanctify. Consider what any sequels to I Play Rocky would potentially have to deal with. Ten years after Rocky made him a star, Stallone is divorced from his wife Sasha Czack, who’s played by AnnaSophia Robb in I Play Rocky and represents his stalwart true love and devoted wife and mother of his first child. In 1985, not long after the divorce from Sasha, Stallone swiftly married model and actor Brigitte Nielsen, who played a role in Rocky IV (1985), written and directed by Stallone. The couple’s short union and ugly divorce began an extended roiling period of Stallone’s personal life that made him a favorite of the tabloid press. His tangled involvements with various models — Janice Dickinson, Angie Everhart, and Jennifer Flavin, whom he married in 1997 — kept supermarket aisle readers entertained for years. Various unsavory accusations of physical and sexual abuse against Stallone by romantic partners that allegedly occurred from the mid-1980s through 2000, including allegations by his own half sister , have kept his lawyers busy through the years. (Stallone denied, and continues to deny, all of the allegations.) As for all the inspirational bonding between Stallone and the tough but ultimately mensch-like producers of Rocky , Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff (played by P. J. Byrne and Toby Kebbell in I Play Rocky ), Stallone’s hatred of Winkler has long been on the record , though he claims to have loved Chartoff. At various points over the years of the franchise, Stallone has called out the elderly Winkler in the media as “remarkably untalented and parasitical,” and accused Winkler’s “moronic vulture children,” Charles and David, of “picking clean the bones” of the Rocky franchise. This feud is based on the original contract that gave the producers an equity stake in a potential franchise but deprived Stallone of one, though he continues to reap other forms of profit from Rocky movies and, of course, is very, very rich. Still, he could always be a bit richer, and it’s a fair enough point — Hollywood contracts are notoriously cutthroat. In I Play Rocky , Stallone doesn’t even read the contract before signing it, much less get a lawyer or agent to look it over. But in I Play Rocky , Winkler and Chartoff go from tough, dismissive Hollywood producers to schmaltzy, huggable slobs, and the film ends with everyone beaming over their shared success. That’s a recognizable emotional trajectory of filmmaking — lots of temporary sentimentalists in the film business giving bear hugs right before the shiv goes in — and it should be noted that both producers really did put up their houses as collateral in order to get studio funding for Rocky . But there’s no indication of the sharp dealing going on or Stallone’s vengeful fury to come. In short, I Play Rocky takes a slightly unusual approach to the biopic — focusing just on the story of Sylvester Stallone getting Rocky made and becoming a star — but otherwise it’s completely typical of the genre. That’s not a compliment, but it hardly matters; audiences love biopics regardless. It’s a shame the biopic isn’t formally classified as a subgenre of fantasy. That would clear up a lot about how these films get made.
