articles.title: American Imperial Decline
articles.author: Tom Engelhardt
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Here’s my question for historians: Has a great imperial power on the downhill slope ever gone quite this crazy before? Given the endless years of human history, it’s not often that you see something that seems truly new (leaving aside, of course, our changing techno-world from electric vehicles to the online universe). In human terms, though, while imperial powers have endlessly risen and fallen, they don’t normally fall with — to give him the credit he deserves — a Donald J. Trump at the helm or a Pete Hegseth as secretary of defense (oops, sorry, war!). And it is remarkable. The country that was once (not so very long ago) arguably the greatest imperial power ever is now being taken into the ditch of history by a uniquely nutty president and crew. Nowhere on Earth is my country truly successful anymore. The half-war it recently fought in Iran was (all too typically) a tactical and literal disaster against a far weaker power (as Michael Klare recently made all too clear in the Nation Magazine ). And thanks to that, less shipping (and so oil and natural gas ) is still coming out of the Strait of Hormuz and energy prices — or just prices generally — though no longer at their peak, remain sky-high . Buy the Book Oh, and don’t forget that “my” popular president and “his” party only recently got thoroughly clobbered in elections across this increasingly unhappy country of ours. The Republicans not only definitively lost a race for senator in Mississippi to a Black Democrat — yes, Mississippi! — for the first time since the Reconstruction era, but in Alaska the Democrats also won the governorship for the first time in almost 30 years. And make no mistake, it was a nationwide vote of rejection, loud and clear, from Americans generally, clearly including many who had once voted for Donald J. Trump. Even Texas went for the Democrats, while that Republican wildcat Lauren Boebert lost in one of Colorado’s most conservative districts! Mind you, having retaken the Senate and House of Representatives in a big-time fashion, the Democrats — despite Bernie and AOC — seem all too likely to reappoint Chuck Shoemar (oops, sorry, Schumer) to lead them in the Senate (again!). So, all too little new there (heaven forbid!) in the age of You Know Exactly Who (or YKEW). You might think that, faced with a human (ir)reality as strange as “our” president on a planet that, in climate change terms, is distinctly going down, down, down (at least when it comes to the conditions that make life on it faintly comfortable), we might be in a far different world. If so, of course, you would underestimate us humans and just what we’re capable (or do I mean incapable?) of doing. As the remarkable Greta Thunberg put it recently, our planet is “not dying, it is being killed and we know by who.” You bet we do (or at least we should)! Long ago, when I was still running TomDispatch.com , I labeled Trump “the president of decline.” Years later, that seems, if anything, all too kind and underwhelming. After all, how often in the past could anyone have said that the greatest power on this planet (even if on the downward slope of history) was being led by — and I don’t think I’m exaggerating here — a distinct nut case, who, in his (unbelievable) second term in office (elected by nearly 50% of American voters), continues to give imperial decline new meaning? Related: Climate Change: The Slow-Motion Atomic Bomb We're Ignoring These days, unfortunately, everything on this planet seems to be growing more extreme and dysfunctional. Among other things, of course, there are the wars that just won’t end, whether in Ukraine (where a Russian drone only recently slammed into a hospital, the National Institute of Traumatology and Orthopedics, in the center of its capital, Kyiv); Gaza {where during a “ceasefire,” as I was writing this, the Israelis sent two missiles into a major medical center, Nasser Hospital, killing six people including, “a child and a prominent surgeon”); or Iran (where numerous health care facilities have similarly been hit by U.S. and Israeli weaponry leading to “at least nine deaths, including that of an infectious diseases health worker and a member of the Iranian Red Crescent Society”). This Planet’s Version of World War III If there’s one thing that doesn’t fully fit the pattern I’ve just described, I would say that it’s the rising imperial power on this failing, flailing planet of ours, China. Unlike more or less every great imperial power in history (including my own, which, since World War II, has fought at least five significant wars — without winning one of them — in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan, Iraq, and now Iran), except for some border skirmishes with India in 2020-2021, China hasn’t fought a significant war in nearly half a century. With distinct foresight, however, it has largely taken over the production of green-power equipment for this overheating planet of ours. To give it full credit, though, when it comes to climate change (which should be considered this planet’s version of World War III), it also remains the most destructive country on Earth by still pouring record amounts of fossil fuels into the atmosphere (though it’s just beginning to cut back on those, too). China aside, the extremity of our distinctly overheating world and of my own country, with its unnervingly overheating president (and crew), remain all too strangely indescribable. Give YKEW credit, in fact. In the weirdest sense imaginable, no words quite fit him. Not truly. He is, in some fashion, simply indescribable. I have little doubt that no descending great power has ever quite had the equivalent of Donald Trump as its leader. And he should also be considered decline personified, which would be a sad enough reality for such a formerly great power. Unfortunately, to give him full credit: he also lends sadness a new meaning on a planet that itself is going down in an unprecedented fashion — or do I mean, in climate-change terms, up (as in flames)? Related: Trump, Climate Change, and the Decline of the American Empire In short, this Trumpian world of... well, I hesitate to say “ours”... still remains all too hard for all too many of us to take in. In 2024, after all, the American people managed to reelect a president (by 1.5% of the popular vote) who, in climate-change terms, remains openly determined to take this planet down with him and that, I believe, should be considered a historical first. It gives the very idea of extremity new meaning. Tom's Substack

articles.title: University of Chicago UE Members Find AI Conference Valuable
articles.content: On Saturday, October 24, six members of UE Local 1103 (GSU-UE), the rank-and-file union of graduate workers at the University of Chicago, attended “Against the AI Campus: Building Power in Higher Ed.” The day-long conference was organized by Higher Ed Labor United (HELU) and held at the University of Illinois Chicago (UIC). The purpose of this conference was to gather workers in higher education together to discuss issues in our workplaces around the burgeoning technology of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and what we can do to protect and expand our worker power. Attendees came from all over the United States and multiple positions in higher education including undergraduate workers, graduate workers, postdocs, non-tenure-track faculty, tenure-track faculty, clerical staff, teaching assistants, operational assistants, and more. The conference began with a discussion defining artificial intelligence, including its history and the recent popular introduction of large language models (LLMs). We discussed how LLMs and other generative AI (GenAI) can be used to degrade or displace our labor in admissions, teaching, research, advising, and evaluation. We then discussed power mapping: tracing through who benefits from the adoption and use of these technologies (the rich and powerful who own the technology) and what pressure points we can use to fight back when we understand these networks of power. We heard from multiple locals who have successfully negotiated language for worker protections related to GenAI into their contracts. The conference concluded with a discussion on how advocacy and legislative action can create real change, especially for public-sector unions. The attendees from UE Local 1103 found many aspects of this conference valuable, especially as we prepare for our upcoming contract negotiations, which will begin in January. The breakout discussions on specific aspects of how GenAI impacts our work (in areas of intellectual property, worker agency, job security, workload, evaluation and discipline, and surveillance) were helpful in modeling discussions we brought back to our own local. Seeing the language other locals won in their contract negotiations provided inspiration for proposals that would unify workers who have very different experiences with GenAI. Worker protections around maintaining the human elements of our relationships with our bosses and our students were especially resonant. Abani Ahmed , a Local 1103 steward in the Computer Science department at the University of Chicago, said, “I really valued hearing from people in all sectors of education, from student to educator and even administration. When thinking about our upcoming contract, it really helped me figure out how to identify the areas that we all agree upon such as the right to refuse the use of AI and the right to have human teachers!” This is not the first time UE higher education locals have participated in discussions on GenAI. In April 2026, leaders from many UE higher ed locals met with staff from the office of Senator Bernie Sanders to discuss how GenAI is impacting our work and how we can protect the dignity of our work in the face of this technology.

articles.title: Gig Economy Is Broken
articles.author: Steven Hill
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Okay, so now the Democrats have impressively won sizable majorities in both the Senate and the House. This moment feels somewhat like the fishbowl ending of the movie “The Candidate,” when the victorious stunned Senator-elect, played by Robert Redford, who has just pulled off a major upset, disorientedly asks his campaign manager, “What do we do now?” Indeed: what will the Democrats do now with their majority? Can they solve real problems for everyday Americans? Governing is a lot harder than defeating a badly wounded rabid candidate like Donald Trump. Here’s an idea that would allow Democrats to solve a real problem that has been hurting many American workers as they grapple with changes in the economy. In recent years, the US labor force has been undergoing a fundamental transformation. In today’s “Uber economy,” self-employed workers, contractors, freelancers, gig workers, temps, permatemps, remote workers after COVID and so-called “independent workers” have been championed by Silicon Valley and Wall Street as the “new way to work”—the wave of the future, especially with AI changing the nature of work itself. Many US consumers have driven in an Uber taxi, but don’t realize that most drivers earn below minimum wage after accounting for vehicle expenses, gas, maintenance, and unpaid time waiting for passengers. Those drivers are so-called “independent contractors,” so the billion-dollar Uber is not responsible for providing healthcare, Social Security contributions, injured worker or unemployment compensation, not to mention sick leave or vacation pay. Related: Women Politicians Under Attack: The Growing Threat to Democracy Another type of “gig-preneur” can be found on platforms like Fiverr, an online job brokerage that connects buyers to sellers of numerous tasks and services called micro-gigs. Each gig pays as little as $5 per job (hence, its Fiverr name). One worker, after fulfilling a total of 27 orders, found that she had made a grand total of $176. “I’ve seen panhandlers get more money outside of the 7-11 ,” she complained. Other types of workers swept up in this job market degradation don’t work at gigs, they have regular jobs. Meet Chris Young, an assembly-line worker at a Nissan manufacturing plant in Tennessee. Young works alongside dozens of other employees doing the exact same job, but he doesn’t work directly for Nissan. Instead, he works as a “perma-temp” for Yates Services, a private contractor who provides a majority of Nissan’s workers. He builds the same Infiniti SUV as the Nissan workers, but he and other Yates employees receive half the salary, less job security, and way fewer safety net benefits. Some “temps” have worked at the same company for as long as 11 years—hence the new term “perma-temp.” How many “new economy” workers are there? America is a wealthy nation, but unfortunately these drastic changes to the job markets have resulted in millions of Americans not enjoying the bounty of that wealth. How many of these new economy workers are there? It’s hard to say because they are difficult to count. The Bureau of Labor Statistics counts about 12 million “independent contractors” (7.4% of 162 million workers in the US) and another 2.8 million (1.7%) on-call workers, over 9 percent of the total workforce. But the BLS uses a narrow “worker” definition, and broader definitions push total estimates much higher, from 16.5 million to over 30 million workers, depending on whether researchers count occasional side gigs or secondary jobs. Industry trackers like MBO Partners estimate that r oughly 75 million Americans (46%) engage in some form of independent work yearly, with 22% treating it as their primary full-time career, more than double the 10% who did so in 2019. Related: Why Are Democrats Shooting Themselves in the Foot on Ranked Choice Voting? New app- and Web-based technologies are making it easier than ever to hire such workers. And there is great incentive for employers to do so, especially in certain industries and occupations, to take advantage of what is known as the “independent contractor loophole.” An employer can lower labor costs dramatically by around 30%, just by evading contributions for a worker’s health benefits, Social Security, Medicare, unemployment, injured workers compensation, lunch breaks, paid sick days and vacation leave. Also, a McKinsey report found that independent contractors get paid 20-30% less than employees. So these savings provides a powerful incentive for an employer to hire as many contractors as possible. To be sure, some businesses legitimately benefit from a degree of labor flexibility, since they need to have an ability to ramp up and down in response to fluctuations in demand for their product or service. But hiring a large contractor workforce allows a company to greatly lower its labor costs by wiping out its workers’ safety net, which undermines a key component that has built the middle class and made the US economy so successful. Portable safety net provides the best of both worlds Fortunately, there is an innovative solution to this tension, and the Democrats should jump on this. It’s called a “portable safety net,” or “portable benefits.” It would allow any worker hired by multiple employers during the year to benefit from a robust safety net. Here’s how it works. Each business who hires an independent worker would contribute a certain amount for that worker, above the wage , that is pro-rated according to the number of hours the worker has worked for that employer. Those payroll deductions would be set aside in an Individual Security Account for each worker, with the funds helping that worker to pay for her/his safety net. The ISA accounts would be structured to direct the payroll deductions into existing federal and state safety net programs—Social Security, Medicare, unemployment insurance and injured workers’ compensation—as well for other safety net components, especially health care, and possibly paid sick days and vacation (the worker also would have some wages deducted, much like regularly-employed full-time workers do). Related: From “11,780 Votes” to Trump’s 2026 Election Power Grab For example, suppose Donna is a regular employee working 20 hours a week for a hairdresser, then contracts for 10 hours a week with TaskRabbit, and drives 10 shifts for Uber. She would earn 50 percent of her benefits from the hairdresser, 25 percent from TaskRabbit, and another percentage based on her wages driving for Uber. The funds from each company would be deposited into her ISA. Note that this is similar to the way Social Security and Obamacare work now, in which a retirement account or a health care account is tracked with a personal ID number for individuals who work for multiple employers. A portable safety net for all workers who need it would result in a number of beneficial effects. It would allow some scheduling flexibility for workers and businesses, as well as the health and financial security that workers and their families need. It also would shore up affordability for many individuals and families, especially after the Trump administration’s deep cuts to Medicaid, Medicare, SNAP and other programs. A portable safety net also would move us beyond all the labor abuses and lawsuits over who’s a contractor or regular employee and entitled to safety net coverage, because all workers would be covered . It would remove the perverse incentive for businesses to use cheaper contractors as a way of lowering their labor costs and undercutting their competitors, which unleashes a race to the bottom. Note that requiring all businesses in an industry to pay into their workers’ ISAs would not hurt the competitiveness of any those businesses, because all employers would be subject to the same rules. The costs for this kind of “safety net insurance plan” could be passed on by businesses to their customers, since that is the largest pool capable of absorbing these costs. Many of the customers would also be the same workers receiving benefits, so it would be a virtuous circle, “a rising tide floating all boats.” A number of countries already do something like this. I first proposed it for American workers back in 2015-16 in my book Raw Deal about the “Uber economy,” and in a policy paper for New America , and the idea sort of caught on in public policy circles . It was endorsed by 40 business, government, labor, and NGO leaders from the right and left who agree: it is a necessary foundation for the 21 st century economy. President Barack Obama endorsed portable benefits in his 2016 State of the Union address, and legislation was proposed in state legislatures in New York, Washington and New Jersey. The idea had some legislative momentum but Trump and COVID killed it. Ironically, the only employers at the time who tried the idea was Uber and Lyft for their California operations, but the Individual Security Accounts they offered were so measly as to be nearly worthless. Rather than paying into the ISA something close to the 20% of a worker’s wage that is necessary to provide an adequate safety net, Uber and Lyft offered only 2.5%. And they required minimum “hours worked” thresholds to qualify that most drivers couldn’t reach. Not surprisingly, Uber/Lyft cynically offered the portable benefits as part of their oppositional campaign, Proposition 22, to overturn a California law, AB 5, that required the companies to treat their drivers like regular employees instead of independent contractors. Related: AI Warfare Goes Unchecked So “portable safety net” was a bit ahead of its time, but none of the salient issues have gone away; in fact the need has only increased as the labor force prepares for the tsunami of AI. In the current moment, this would be a great issue for the Democrats to champion. Already there is momentum building in various states . A portable safety net for all workers is an idea whose time has come. It would help ensure that the labor force and the broader economy are placed on a fair and healthy foundation for the future. All Americans deserve to be enriched by technology and innovation, instead of made obsolete or impoverished by it. For the Democrats, this has the makings of a win-win solution. But are Democratic leaders bold enough to seize the opportunity? DemocracySOS

articles.title: New Nuclear Arms Race
articles.author: Vijay Prashad
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. On 19 November, President Xi Jinping of China hosted a meeting with President Vladimir Putin of Russia and President Donald Trump of the United States. They met in Shenzhen at the margins of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum. The final statement that appeared from them had a very powerful line, ‘A nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought’. This line came from three of the most important nuclear weapons countries in the world, only one of which – the United States – had used a nuclear bomb against civilians (in Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945). The other nuclear weapons countries (France, India, Israel, North Korea, Pakistan, and the United Kingdom) do not have the scale of the arsenals of the three that met in Shenzhen, which means that they do not have the capacity for a full nuclear war; for most of them, the nuclear weapons are a deterrent against the destruction of their state by others. The statement from these three powers, then, is indicative of the mood toward a new agreement on the danger and futility of nuclear weapons. The earliest treaty around the use of nuclear weapons was signed on 1 December 1959. This Antarctic Treaty banned nuclear explosions and radioactive waste disposal in Antarctica. It was followed on 5 December 1963 with the Partial Test Ban Treaty between the USSR, the United States, and the United Kingdom. This second treaty prohibited nuclear explosions in the atmosphere, in outer space, and underwater, while leaving underground testing permitted (this was eventually banned by the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test Ban Treaty of 10 September 1996, although the major nuclear powers have not signed onto it yet). Over the past sixty-seven years, we saw an increase in treaties to manage the diabolical presence of nuclear weapons for the first decades, and then we saw a collapse of the entire nuclear management machinery. That machinery has been dismantled piece by piece. The Shenzhen meeting is the first in very many years that revives the language of the danger of nuclear war and should be built upon by all peace-loving people. Related: Global Left Rising: From Trump's Defeat to Lula's Victory in Brazil The Collapse of Nuclear Weapons Management On 5 February 2026, New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) expired. Signed in 2010 and extended in 2021, this treaty had restricted deployed US and Russian strategic nuclear forces and provided mechanisms for verification. It is the last of the treaties that manage the nuclear weapons arsenals of the nuclear weapons states to lapse. There are now no binding numerical limits on the nuclear weapons arsenals. Reacting to this, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said , ‘For the first time in more than half a century, we face a world without any binding limits on the strategic nuclear arsenals’. It would be inaccurate to say that no nuclear weapons agreements remain. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty continues to exist, as do other nuclear treaties and obligations. The specific danger is that the two states possessing the largest arsenals (the USA and Russia) no longer operate under a binding bilateral ceiling on their strategic nuclear forces. Assurances of restraint cannot replace inspections, exchanges of information, agreed definitions, and enforceable limits. Political understandings can disappear with a change of government or a deterioration in relations. That is why the Shenzhen statement is significant, but only if it rebuilds a new treaty between these countries. The record of what has been lost is sobering: First. The Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty, signed in 1972, limited missile defence systems and helped to anchor the strategic relationship between Washington and Moscow. The United States withdrew on 13 June 2002 when US President George W. Bush decided to take advantage of temporary Russian weakness to advance the goals of US power. Whatever the limited promise made for missile defence, the abandonment of negotiated restraints encouraged adversaries to seek new means of overcoming those defences. Military spending, a waste of social wealth, began to balloon upwards. Second. The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, signed in 1987, eliminated US and Soviet ground-launched missiles with ranges between 500 and 5,500 kilometres. Washington withdrew from the treaty on 2 August 2019, when President Trump decided to press further US advantages against Russia. An entire category of weapons, once removed through negotiation, returned to military planning. This withdrawal further cornered Russia and provoked the invasion of eastern Ukraine. These two examples are the culmination of years of erosion across several areas of arms control. But they are the most significant treaties to have been set aside, and therefore put the world into a new arms race, particularly a new nuclear arms race. These agreements were a product of fear and political calculation. They were needed to understand that an adversary’s insecurity could become everyone’s catastrophe. In that sense, the inspections and the restrictions operated as confidence building measures across disagreements. Their destruction has restored a dangerous dependence on threat assessments, intelligence estimates, and the judgment of leaders operating under pressure. At Shenzhen, three leaders did not announce any reductions, verification arrangements, or timetable for negotiations, but they have established a political opening through which a peace agenda could be rebuilt. China’s participation adds an important dimension, since Beijing has not been a party to most of these bilateral treaties. A durable framework must address Beijing’s security concerns as well as those of Washington and Moscow. Humanity cannot afford to dismiss an opening for negotiation because it falls short of an agreement. Related: India's Mediterranean Strategy: Warships, Billionaires, and NATO Europe’s Absence The absence of Europe at the meeting in Shenzhen is notable. Rather than accept the deescalation that could result from the meeting in China, the European leaders gathered in Berlin for a Coalition of the Willing meeting. This name, Coalition of the Willing, comes from a platform developed by retired UK politician Keir Starmer in March 2025, with the stated purpose for European leaders to support Ukraine’s military. If in Shenzhen the three major powers spoke of their concern for nuclear war and war in general, at Berlin the Europeans spoke of increased military expenditure, weapons deliveries, and an increased pressure campaign against Russia. Coalition members reaffirmed a pledge of €70 billion in military equipment, assistance, and training for Ukraine in 2026, with at least equivalent support in 2027. They proposed stronger economic pressure on Russia and discussed a European-led multinational force, supported by the United States, to operate after a ceasefire. These commitments extended the material infrastructure of confrontation. Shenzhen focused on de-escalation through engagement, while Berlin put the matter of escalation of military commitments firmly on the table. The European leaders’ talk of military expenditure came as their own populations took to the streets to condemn the austerity agenda that would make Europe more impoverished and more insecure. There was no public mention of these protests, nor was their acknowledgement that their agenda has very low public support . Opposition to the agenda of increase military spending and increased social austerity reaches 63 percent in Italy, 59 percent in Austria, 56 percent in Germany, and 55 percent in Estonia. The statement itself is anodyne, asking for greater military spending and for Russian concessions but it does not spell out a broad plan for European security. The entire agenda relies upon Europe’s dependency on Washington for crucial military capabilities and diplomatic access. This makes the Berlin agenda utterly unsustainable. Related: The Red Sea War Economy: How Foreign Powers Profit While Africa Suffers BRICS+ Agenda The opening of new negotiations for nuclear weapons control carries particular significance for the BRICS+ agenda. Countries outside the principal military blocs would bear devastating consequences from a confrontation they neither initiated nor controlled. Their interest in reducing nuclear danger is direct, which is why they should press for negotiations rather than leave the issue to an exclusive conversation among the largest powers. China and Russia attended Shenzhen in their national capacities. Their participation did not give them a mandate to bargain for the entire Global South. The test is whether their diplomacy creates greater room for other countries to pursue development, trade, and independent foreign policies. Reduced confrontation could open that space; an arrangement protecting only the privileges of powerful states would narrow its promise. BRICS+ has already connected disarmament to its practical development agenda. Resources consumed by arms races are unavailable for public health, housing, ecological repair, and productive investment. Its institutions can widen access to finance while its members demand that the nuclear powers fulfil their responsibilities. The New Development Bank’s pursuit of lending in members’ national currencies illustrates one avenue for increasing countries’ economic options. At the 19th BRICS+ Summit to be held in China, the issue of the trade-off between development and war will likely be further discussed. Shenzhen’s importance lies in the possibility it reopened. Three nuclear powers acknowledged a shared danger at a moment when binding restraints have disappeared. The task now is to make their acknowledgment material: negotiations, verification, limits, and reductions. Humanity needs an international movement strong enough to insist that the next announcement concerns weapons withdrawn and agreements signed, rather than another budget for preparing the war no society can survive. This article was produced by Globetrotter and No Cold War .

articles.title: The US-Israel Relationship Is Shifting. Not Nearly Enough.
articles.author: Gilbert Achcar
articles.content: On November 3, the very day of the midterm congressional elections, Donald Trump announced that the United States would cease its annual military aid to Israel at the end of this year. That aid, amounting to $3.8 billion annually, was provided under an agreement signed by the Obama administration in 2016, covering the ten years from 2019 through 2028. Trump cannot end it on his own — the money is appropriated by Congress — but the announcement was no surprise: it had been signaled before, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, now leading a caretaker government after Israel’s October election, said he was fine with it (or pretended to be), arguing that the Zionist state no longer needs this money and is perfectly capable of purchasing US weapons at its own expense. The truth is that US military aid to Israel, as to other countries — regional states like Egypt and Jordan in particular — consists essentially of funding those governments’ purchase of US weaponry. In other words, it is an old and familiar method of using American taxpayers’ money to fund and enrich the military-industrial complex, one of the largest sectors of American capitalism. The regular annual aid to Israel, moreover, is only a floor: Washington readily raises the amount when circumstances call for it. A report published last year found that the United States provided Israel with $21.7 billion in military aid during the first two years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, under the Biden and then the Trump administrations. That is but one measure of Washington’s full complicity in the genocide. Still, the talk of ending the annual aid is significant, particularly given the timing. Everyone understood that, by making the announcement on Election Day, the president was attempting to mitigate the considerable damage done to his party by his enthusiastic support for Israel and his constant praise of Netanyahu at a time when the war on Gaza has shifted American public opinion, which is outraged at the spectacle of Israeli cruelty toward the Palestinians. A Public That Has Turned A Washington Post –Ipsos poll conducted last July revealed that 55 percent of the public now considers US military aid to Israel excessive, including 29 percent who support ending it completely, while 26 percent wish to see it reduced. According to another poll conducted last September, the proportion of those favorable to Israel in US public opinion has plummeted to 29 percent, its lowest level to date, while 59 percent declare holding an unfavorable view. And another recent poll, published last July, shows that 58 percent of young Americans under thirty (including 72 percent of young Democrats) sympathize with the Palestinian people nowadays, compared to 32 percent who sympathize with their Israeli oppressor. These figures make inevitable a shift in the relationship between the Zionist state and its US godfather. The question is, what will be the nature of this shift? Netanyahu has boasted that the end of the funding marks a transition from dependency to an alliance of equals. The truth is that Israel would benefit from reducing its dependence on Washington, freeing itself as much as possible from the looming prospect of US pressure. That concern is all the more pressing for Israel given the shift in American public opinion and the Republicans’ debacle in the midterms, which cost them control of both houses of Congress. One should not, however, be overly optimistic about the future of the relationship. The share of leftists among congressional Democrats has grown to an unprecedented degree, but the Democratic majority does not share their principled position: refusing to supply the Zionist state with US weapons at all, even at its own expense — or at least restricting the kind of weapons supplied and imposing strict conditions on their use, on Israel’s conduct in the Palestinian territories occupied in 1967 and, more generally, on its aggressive and expansionist regional policies. The Liberal Zionist Ceiling A glimpse of where the Democratic majority’s position on Israel might be heading, should current trends continue, is offered by a policy agenda that J Street, the liberal Zionist lobby, published this November. Founded in 2008 as a rival to the much older, right-wing American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), whose origins date to 1954, J Street has gained significant influence at its rival’s expense over the past two years. Its proposal calls for treating Israel like any other wealthy ally — selling it weapons rather than subsidizing them. It still supports supplying Israel with defensive missiles like the Iron Dome, the product of cooperation between the US and Israeli military-industrial complexes, a collaboration J Street sees no problem with — so long as Israel pays. As for the political conditions J Street would impose on the Israeli government, they include support for “elements” of the Gaza “peace plan” that the Trump administration produced last year — with an emphasis on disarming Hamas on the one hand and freezing the expansion of Zionist settlements in the West Bank on the other. The document also calls on Israel to commit to the prospect of a “State of Palestine” alongside it. That has nominally been Washington’s policy for years, including Trump’s: the plan drafted by Jared Kushner and unveiled by the president in January 2020, the final year of his first term, in Netanyahu’s presence and to his effusive praise. Pressure From Below Of course, even a shift in US policy in such a direction, should it occur, would have a beneficial impact despite its obvious limitations. But US foreign policy is primarily managed by the president, meaning that Trump will continue to shape it for the remaining two years of his term. Left-wing pressure for a radical change in US policy toward Israel must continue and grow, in public opinion and in Congress, building on the ongoing momentum — to stop the United States from arming Israel and to force a fundamental change in its treatment of the Palestinian people. Deepening the shift in US policy toward Israel is a prerequisite for a change among Israeli Jews, and reversing the drift to the far right that has dominated their society since the turn of the century and accelerated dangerously after the Hamas-led operation of October 7, 2023. Without that change, there can be no relief for the Palestinian people from the unbearable suffering inflicted on them and no real prospect of their achieving their fundamental, inalienable right to self-determination — without which no durable peace is possible in the Middle East. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Black Political Power Rising
articles.author: Erin Aubry Kaplan
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The ultimate meaning of the midterms is still unfolding, but one thing’s for sure: It was a hell of a moment for Black representation. After all the obstacles the GOP threw in the path of Black voting in the South, from stringent voter ID laws to stacked election boards, when the dust had settled the seemingly impossible had happened: Black women had won multiple statewide seats in Georgia, including governor; five Black people were elected governor, a historic high; and Scott Colom took a Senate seat in Mississippi, the first time a Black man has been elected senator in Mississippi since Reconstruction. Black voting surged after organizers and leaders across the country, from Black Votes Matter to the NAACP, worked furiously to increase turnout. Donald Trump may still be in charge but the message across the country is clear: politically, Black is back. But not in L.A. Karen Bass, the city’s first Black female mayor, lost to Councilmember Nithya Raman. It was quite a reversal of fortune: After being hailed as a historymaker and purveyor of progressive change in 2022, Bass, 73, was rejected by voters this time around as inept and too establishment. That rejection was certainly part of a national embrace of big change that didn’t favor incumbents — as Bass said in her own analysis of her loss. But for some people in L.A. it marks something else: a low point in Black political power and presence in civic life. When the new mayor and city council is sworn in next month, L.A. will see its number of Black elected officials cut in half, from four to two. Dermot Givens, a longtime campaign consultant who’s worked with generations of candidates, including Bass, said the loss of Black representation isn’t only in elected office, but also in leadership on the ground, where it all starts. “The midterms results were very exciting elsewhere in the country, especially the South,” said Givens. “Really positive. But it’s over for Black folks in L.A.” That sounds jarring. Despite a declining Black population, which stands at about 8% today, and ongoing racial disparities, L.A. is still viewed by many as the city of possibilities, long home to the largest Black middle class in the West. Related: Blue Wave Rejected Trump: Did It Also Reject Racism? But that’s optics. Black community leaders with real constituencies who have traditionally been the bridge to political power — leaders with what Givens calls “gravitas” — are all but gone, he said. And he sees Bass’ failure as proof. “Ninety-nine percent of the Black establishment backed Karen and she still lost,” said Givens, referring to Black elected officials and other political figures who supported Bass’ reelection. “That speaks to the fact the people weren’t connected to the establishment. They weren’t motivated.” It’s true that the energy that powered Bass’ bid for mayor in 2022 simply was not there in 2026. One thing that helped four years ago was that her opponent was Rick Caruso, a white, wealthy developer and former Republican. The contrast between them gave voters a stark political choice; this year’s contest between Raman, a woman of color and a progressive Democrat like Bass, was less about politics and more about personal competence and who could best lead the city. It was also about exciting voters. Even among the Black voters who supported Bass, there was an enthusiasm problem . Of course, there were voters who were genuinely excited about Bass. Stephen Townsend, 56, said the reason he went to the polls at all on Nov. 3 was to reelect her. “I’ve met her before in person, and I got a feeling she’s a decent, genuine person,” said Townsend, who lives in Leimert Park and manages video game production at Amazon. Noting her deep roots as a community organizer, he said that “she’s been a big part of the community for so long. She’s not pretending to be here. And she’s still trying to do the right thing.” Related: Does Karen Bass Still Deserve the Support of Black Los Angeles? Bass’ defeat speaks to the dearth of Black leaders who can rally the community around a candidate or issue, Givens said — a pastor like the civic-minded Cecil Murray of First A.M.E. Church or a politician like Mark Ridley-Thomas whose South L.A. Empowerment Congress prefigured neighborhood councils. (Murray died in 2024 and Ridley-Thomas was convicted in 2023 of federal conspiracy and bribery charges). But he said those efforts have fallen off as Black leadership over the years has become more personality-driven and less focused on building Black solidarity that could be sustained into the future. “Nithya Raman is an immigrant who stood up for immigrants in being against the current police chief because of LAPD’s involvement with ICE. But Karen didn’t stand up for Black people that way,” said Givens. “She just didn’t.” Givens thinks Black solidarity in L.A. has been ebbing since the ’70s, the golden age of Black politics that officially launched when Tom Bradley was elected the city’s first Black mayor in 1973. He served for the next 20 years. “We had everything going in L.A. then” — including a Black population that peaked at about 18% in 1970 — “but it never expanded,” Givens said. “It turns out that it wasn’t about building anything. Black people got complacent. We thought white people would take care of us.” Now, he said, with Bass on the way out and no up-and-coming Black candidates in sight, “There’s zero political future here.” He added: “And politically, other groups in power, they don’t need us.” None of this means Black people in L.A. have disappeared, or don’t have urgent concerns that can and should be addressed by the incoming mayor and city council. Raman is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, an organization whose ranks are well represented on the city council. Its agenda overlaps with much of what Black folks want, from increasing affordable housing to expanding the social safety net to achieving real racial equality. In the final week of the campaign, Raman released a Black agenda . Among the pledges she makes are to address renters’ concerns, grow Black businesses and “center Black voices at City Hall.” It’s a promise of inclusion that, ironically, reminds us of just how diminished those voices have become. After next month, only two Black councilmembers will remain: Heather Hutt and Marqueece Harris-Dawson, the council president, who is facing a recall campaign generated in part by irate Black constituents who say he has failed them. And a Latino will represent Council District 9 in South Central, which had Black representation since 1963. Related: Destination Crenshaw: Can a $150 Million Art Project Save Black Los Angeles? Latino voters helped Bass prevail in the primary, but their dramatic shift to Raman in the general election proved decisive. For many Black Angelenos, the memory of how Latino politicians and power brokers tossed around racist insults during a backroom discussion in 2022 while casually speculating on Black people’s political demise is still fresh. And while those responsible paid the price — Kevin de León, one of those brokers, was voted off the city council — still unanswered was the question about how Black people will fare in a city where their numbers and political influence have declined. Bass’ election that year answered the question, for a while. Her exit makes it urgent again. Yet Bass deserves some credit. Whatever she failed to do as mayor, as the city’s first woman of color to be elected to the position, she broke through a wall that Raman stepped through easily. Like Bradley, she will be remembered as a barrier breaker. But both of them left office with Black communities in crisis, or at serious inflection points — Bradley after the massive unrest of 1992, Bass in the midst of a crushing affordable housing crisis driving gentrification and homelessness that’s disproportionately impacting Black residents and their sense of a stake in a future here. Givens said the only way forward is for Black Angelenos to organize themselves and hold Raman accountable to an agenda of their own. Without the leadership infrastructure of old, it won’t be easy. But not impossible. Townsend, for his part, is optimistic. Related: We Had Been Friends for 50 Years.
